title: a bot that beats freedoom
what: people keep saying ai can do almost anything, and a bot that plays a whole doom level is a simple, public way to check. it's also fun to watch. in the 2025 videogamebench test, the best ai models barely got out of the first room of doom ii. vizdoom lets a bot see the screen plus a few helper views like a depth map. build an open bot that finds the keys in real freedoom levels and reaches the exit alive, so anyone can rerun it and see where game-playing ai really stands.
done_when: an open bot finishes freedoom phase 2 maps 1 to 8 from a pistol start on skill 3, using only vizdoom's screen, depth, label and automap buffers, with eight recorded demos that replay to the exit on other people's machines.

runs.command: python replay.py demos/ (replays each MAP01-MAP08 demo in vizdoom 1.3 and prints whether the exit was reached and the time, and exits 0 only when all eight demos reach the exit)

people.instructions: watch at least two replays at full speed. note any wall clipping, god mode or other cheat, and confirm the bot used no map data beyond the allowed buffers by reading its input code.

why_now: vizdoom 1.3.1 shipped in september 2026, and full single-player doom levels with keys and switches are still a hard target for bots.

title: kart race on the moon
what: almost nobody will ever stand on the moon, but anyone could drive through a real piece of it. it's a silly, lovely way for a kid to learn the shape of a real place up there. nasa mapped the apollo 17 landing valley at 2 meters per pixel, and you can download it. turn the valley into a supertuxkart track, so you can race tux past the real hills where astronauts drove the lunar rover in 1972.
done_when: a supertuxkart 1.5 track built from nasa's apollo 17 terrain model is live on the supertuxkart add-ons site under cc-by-sa 4.0, and ai karts can finish a three-lap race on it.

runs.command: ./check-heights.py track/ NAC_DTM_APOLLO17_2M.tif (samples 1,000 points and confirms the track terrain matches the scaled nasa heights)

people.instructions: race three laps against ai karts. compare the horizon with an apollo 17 photo and say whether it feels like the place.

builds_on: SuperTuxKart https://github.com/supertuxkart/stk-code + LROC NAC Apollo 17 DTM https://data.lroc.im-ldi.com/lroc/view_rdr_product/NAC_DTM_APOLLO17_2M
why_now: supertuxkart 1.5 came out in october 2025, and lroc terrain models of every apollo site are free to download.
needs_humans: blender track builders and texture artists who can make grey dust look good.

title: minecraft in doom
what: this one is for fun, and anyone can play it free: no copy of doom or minecraft needed. freedoom's first nine maps, rebuilt block for block in uzdoom, the active fork of gzdoom. you're a blocky marine, and every wall can be dug through, so you can tunnel around a fight instead of through it. what you mine you can place again or craft with, and the shotgun you pick up lands in a minecraft-style inventory. freedoom's monsters share the maps with new blocky ones in minecraft's spirit, all there to be blown apart. picture an imp that sneaks up and blows a hole in your wall the way a creeper would, or monsters stitched together from imps and zombies. there's no build phase: you play the maps straight through. it takes pixel artists, mappers and playtesters together, and the hard part is holding 60 fps with thousands of diggable blocks on screen.
done_when:
a downloadable uzdoom mod rebuilds freedoom phase 1 maps e1m1 to e1m9 entirely from blocks, and:

- every wall can be dug out
- gathered blocks can be placed again or crafted with at least 10 recipes
- guns you pick up sit in a minecraft-style inventory
- freedoom's monsters fight beside at least 4 new blocky ones drawn fresh, including an imp-like one with its own name that explodes and blows holes in block walls
- each map can be finished from a pistol start on skill 3
- it holds 60 fps on the reference rig (a ryzen 5 3600 with a gtx 1660 at 1080p)
- it uses only freedoom and other open assets

runs.command: ./bench.sh (on the reference rig, plays the bundled benchmark demo through e1m1 to e1m9 in uzdoom with freedoom1.wad and prints min and average fps, and exits non-zero if the minimum is under 60) && ./demos.sh (plays one pistol-start demo per map on skill 3 and prints whether each reached the exit, and exits non-zero if any map's demo doesn't) && ./audit.sh mcdoom.pk3 (counts the crafting recipes and the new monster classes, and lists, per map, any wall that isn't built from blocks or can't be dug out, and exits non-zero with fewer than 10 recipes, fewer than 4 new monster classes, or any wall listed) && ./license-scan.sh mcdoom.pk3 (exits non-zero if any file in the mod isn't from freedoom or under an open license)

people.instructions: download the mod from its public link and play e1m1 and one later map from a pistol start for 15 minutes each: dig through a wall, mine blocks, place one again and craft at least one thing from them, pick up a gun and check it sits in the inventory, and blow up every kind of monster you meet, including the exploding imp-like one; check it has its own name in the game (not imp, serpentipede or creeper) and that it blows holes in block walls. post your fps, any block you could walk through or that broke or placed wrong, and any texture, sound or monster that looks taken from doom or minecraft rather than drawn fresh. at least one tester must be human.

builds_on: uzdoom (gpl, active gzdoom fork) https://github.com/UZDoom/UZDoom + freedoom (bsd) https://github.com/freedoom/freedoom
why_now: uzdoom 5.0.3 shipped in september 2026 while gzdoom itself has had no release since may 2025. the closest mod, voxel violence, stalled at v0.3 in 2022; it needs doom ii and adds blocks only on top of normal maps, with no digging through whole levels, crafting or new monsters.
needs_humans: pixel artists to draw blocks, guns and monsters by hand, mappers to rebuild nine maps block for block, and playtesters who can feel a bad hitbox in ten seconds.

title: a $30 seismometer in 1000 homes
what:
most people who live with earthquakes have no seismometer anywhere near them. in 2017 a quake of about magnitude 4.6 shook the desert in northern niger, and the closest open station, about 600 km away in algeria, happened to be off. a finished home seismograph like the raspberry shake rs1d costs about $585 assembled, so few homes have one, though stanford's quake-catcher network showed that cheap sensors in homes and schools catch real quakes.

we research what hosts need, design a sensor that's cheap to make, make it, and ship it finished, ready to plug in, so a home in lima or kathmandu can join as easily as one in tokyo. the target is under $30 a unit all in, and $25 is the stretch aim. that's realistic: the sensing and wifi chips cost a few dollars, and a finished device with its board, power, case, assembly, testing and shipping lands around $20 to $30 at a run of a few thousand.

the goal is 1000 homes in 20 countries: quakes strike along many separate fault lines, from the pacific rim to the himalaya and east africa, and a device that only clears one country's customs, plugs and radio rules hasn't really been shipped to the world. every station streams to one open map where anyone can watch the ground move, and the network is a base for early warning later. it takes hardware and firmware designers, seismologists, people who can run production and shipping, and hosts in many countries.
done_when:
a finished home seismometer with an open design:

- is made for under $30 a unit all in (parts, case, power supply, assembly and shipping, on an open cost sheet)
- is running in at least 1000 homes in at least 20 countries, each delivered ready to plug in and set up by its host with no tools
- and from the stations' public data alone, the network detects at least 20 magnitude 4+ earthquakes that usgs also lists, each at 2 or more stations within 60 seconds of usgs's origin time.

runs.command: python check_network.py network.toml
runs.description: reads the public station list and waveform archive named in network.toml, re-runs the open detector on that data, matches its detections to usgs's magnitude 4+ catalog through the fdsn api, and counts live stations, homes and countries; it exits 0 only at 1000 or more homes in 20 or more countries and 20 or more matched magnitude 4+ quakes, each seen at 2 or more stations within 60 seconds of usgs's origin time

people.instructions: pick 3 hosts in different countries from the station list. confirm with each, by email or a call, that the device arrived finished, that setup took no tools, and that it's still streaming. check the cost sheet's totals against the linked invoices for one production run, then pick 3 detected quakes and confirm them on usgs's site.

why_now: grillo and ibm released openeew, an open sensor with detection code, in 2020, and it's still public under apache 2.0. its sensor repository has been almost quiet since 2021 (one commit in august 2025 added kicad project files), so the crowd starts from a working design and spends its effort on cost, finish and shipping.
needs_humans: hardware and firmware designers, seismologists to tune detection, people who can run production batches and ship them across borders, and hosts in quake-prone places in at least 20 countries.

title: the hand-drawn world
what: everyone carries a map of their own neighborhood in their head. draw yours by hand, on paper or on a screen, the way you'd sketch it for a friend. we pin each drawing to openstreetmap at a few matching corners, so the sketches sit where they belong, and a world map grows out of the places people actually know.
done_when: a public web map shows at least 30 hand-drawn neighborhood maps by 30 different people in at least 5 countries, each warped onto openstreetmap from at least 4 matching points with an average error under 25 meters, and every drawing is under an open license.

runs.command: python check_fit.py drawings/
runs.description: recomputes each drawing's average error at its matching points against openstreetmap and checks the counts: 30 drawings, 30 people, 5 countries, open licenses; it exits 0 only when every count is met and each drawing's average error is under 25 meters

people.instructions: open the map and compare 10 random drawings with the openstreetmap street layout underneath. confirm each is hand-drawn (not traced from the map) and sits on the right streets.

builds_on: openstreetmap (odbl) https://www.openstreetmap.org, with map warping in gdal or qgis georeferencer (open source)
why_now: phones make it easy to photograph a paper sketch, and open georeferencing tools can pin it to real streets in minutes. a map of how people see their own streets doesn't exist anywhere.
needs_humans: people in many countries who will draw their own neighborhood by hand. that part can't be generated.

title: where am i? ask the birds
what:
it's geoguessr by ear, and anyone with a phone can play. the birds singing outside your window give away where you are: which species live there, and even their regional accents. models like birdnet and google's perch can already name the species, but the best published model for placing a sound on the map is still off by about 1,000 km on a typical clip.

train a model that hears one minute of outdoor sound and guesses where on earth it was recorded, then test it on fresh minutes from all over the world that it never heard. the fresh minutes can come from a shared dawn-chorus day, when people everywhere record the same morning. a model that knows which birds sing where also shows what bird models really know about the world, and every minute recorded for the test is a dated note of what was singing where. it takes people recording in many countries, birders to check what's singing, and model builders.
done_when:
a model anyone can download and run hears one minute of outdoor sound and guesses where on earth it was recorded, and:

- on at least 200 new one-minute recordings, made after the shwarm opens by at least 50 people in at least 20 countries and hidden from the model until scoring by a scorer who builds no model here, named in the thread before recording starts, who posts the set's sha256 when collecting closes, its median error is under 500 km
- 3 people on 3 different continents each record a fresh minute where they stand, and the model places each one within 500 km

runs.command: python score.py model/ hidden-set/
runs.description: runs the model on every hidden recording and prints the median distance error, counts the recordings, recorders and countries, checks that each recording was made after the shwarm opened, and checks that the model's sha256 was posted before the hidden set was released to the scorer run; it exits 0 only when the median error is under 500 km over at least 200 recordings by at least 50 people in at least 20 countries

people.instructions: read the three live-test posts. confirm they come from 3 different continents, that each person recorded a fresh minute outdoors where they stood and ran the model on it, and that each guess landed within 500 km of where they were. confirm the hidden set was held by a scorer outside the model's builders and that the model scored is the one whose hash was posted first. then record your own minute outside and post how far off the model was.

why_now: in 2025 a team at umass amherst published the first big test of placing natural sounds on a map: their best model was off by a median of about 1,080 km on single clips of around 20 seconds, and about 520 km when it pooled recordings from the same place and time. google's perch 2.0, trained on over 1.5 million animal recordings, came out in august 2025. the pieces exist; nobody has tried them on fresh minutes recorded around the world.
needs_humans: people in at least 20 countries to record one minute of outdoor sound each for the hidden test set, 3 people on different continents for the live test, birders to check species, and model builders.

title: rediscover all seven trappist-1 planets in raw k2 pixels
what: finding planets around other stars sounds like a job for big observatories, but the data is public, and one clear worked example would let a student or a curious adult learn how it's done. in early 2017, kepler's k2 mission stared at trappist-1 for 79 days. buried in that noisy data were 4 transits of the outermost planet, enough for luger et al. to pin down its 18.77 day orbit. this is a rediscovery, not a new find: start from the raw pixels, find all seven planets without peeking, and leave an open notebook anyone can learn planet hunting from.
done_when: an open notebook starting from the k2 campaign 12 target pixel file recovers the periods of all seven planets within 0.1% of luger et al. 2017, using a blind search with no period priors.

runs.command: jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute trappist_blind.ipynb && python check_periods.py (compares the seven periods the notebook found with luger et al. 2017, and exits 0 only when all seven are within 0.1%)

people.instructions: read the notebook and confirm no published period or transit time is used before the search step.

why_now: the data has been public since 2017, and open tools now make a blind search a weekend project for a small crew.
needs_humans: an astronomer to catch false signals from k2's thruster firings and flares.

title: measure the earth with sticks in 10 cities
what: around 240 bc, eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two egyptian cities and worked out the size of the earth. we have phones and friends on every continent. how close can a stick in the ground get us?
done_when: on one agreed day, at least 10 people at different latitudes post photos of a vertical stick's noon shadow with measurements, and the combined estimate of earth's pole-to-pole circumference lands within 1% of 40,008 km.

runs.command: python fit_earth.py shadows.csv

people.instructions: check each photo shows a plumb-checked stick with a tape at the shadow tip, and that its time stamp is near local solar noon.

why_now: anyone with a stick can join, and a crew can finish in one sunny day.
needs_humans: people spread across many latitudes, ideally on both sides of the equator.

title: a tile with heesch number 7
what: this one is for the joy of a good puzzle: a new record in a question about tiles that mathematicians have chewed on for decades. some tiles can't cover the plane, yet copies can still ring them a few times over. the record is 6 full rings, found by bojan bašić in 2021. we search polyforms for one that takes 7. a find would be a small, real piece of new math, and every dead end we publish saves other hunters the trouble.
done_when: isohedral/heesch-sat classifies a connected, hole-free unmarked polyform as a non-tiler with heesch number at least 7, and the witness file is public.

runs.command: ./sat -show -maxlevel 20 tile.txt -o out.txt && ./report out.txt | grep -Eq 'with Hc = ([7-9]|[1-9][0-9])$'
runs.description: sat and report are heesch-sat's own tools; this exits 0 only when report lists a non-tiler with a hole-free heesch number of at least 7

why_now: kaplan's sat-based tool makes huge searches cheap, and epoch lists heesch number 7 as an open challenge.
needs_humans: an eye for which tile families are worth searching.

title: explain one ai proof to a human
what: on oct 6, openai posted 722 math papers written by its models, and about 42% of their main results are checked in lean. a lean check tells us a proof is correct. it doesn't tell anyone why the proof works. terence tao calls this an open exposition problem, a proof that's known to work and still waits for an explanation a person can follow ([terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/10/10/math-2-0](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/10/10/math-2-0/)). one of those papers settles the 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... case of the erdős similarity problem (#120), which ben green lists as his problem 94, and its main theorem is lean-checked. it's 16 pages and nobody has explained it yet. write the version a person can follow: where the idea comes from, why each step works, and what breaks without it.
done_when: an explanation of openai's 'the dyadic case of the erdős similarity conjecture' is published under cc by 4.0, and a reader who hadn't read the paper explains its key step in their own words and says they could rebuild the argument from the explanation alone.

people.instructions: don't read the paper first. read the explanation, then write in your own words how the 'net' catches every copy of 1, 1/2, 1/4, ... at every scale, and why the leftover set still has almost all of [0,1]. flag any step that only restates the paper without saying why it works. pass if you could rebuild the argument from the explanation.

why_now: the proofs arrived on oct 6, faster than anyone can read them, and tao's math 2.0 talk on oct 9 asked for exactly this kind of work.
needs_humans: a human reader is the whole point: an explanation only counts once a person follows it. measure theory and a little probability are enough to read the paper.

title: beat one bound in tao's table
what:
it's a rare chance for someone outside a math department to add a real, checked result to mathematics. two of them, and where they sit now:

| constant | lower bound | upper bound |
|---|--:|--:|
| erdős minimum overlap | 0.379005 | 0.380868 |
| shannon capacity of the 7-cycle | 3.2588 | 3.3177 |

tao's repo tracks over a hundred constants like these, and many give way to clever computer search. pick one and move a number, with a certificate a stranger can check.
done_when: a pull request that improves the best known upper or lower bound on any constant in `teorth/optimizationproblems` is merged, backed by a certificate that a stranger can check with one script.

runs.command: gh pr view <the pull request's url> --json state --jq .state | grep -qx MERGED && python3 verify.py certificate.json   # verify.py is the submission's own checker; it prints the new bound and exits 0 only when the certificate gives a bound better than the table's

why_now: the table started in january 2026 and is still getting fresh records, so the easy wins are not all gone.
needs_humans: choosing which constant is ripe, and writing up the bound so a referee can follow it.

title: beat the open solar forecast
what: a better guess at tomorrow's sun helps people with rooftop panels decide when to charge a battery or a car, so more of their own clean power gets used. open climate fix's quartz forecast tells anyone with panels how many kw to expect over the next 48 hours, free. its default model misses by about 0.19 kw on the public test set of 50 uk sites. cut that error and every home battery or ev charger that reads it plans a little better.
done_when: a pull request to open-source-quartz-solar-forecast scores at least 10% lower overall mae than the default gradient boosting model at commit c07ad74 (0.1906 kw in its readme), so under 0.1715 kw on the first "MAE:" line scripts/run_evaluation.py prints, using no data from after forecast time.

runs.command: git clone <fork> && cd open-source-quartz-solar-forecast && pip install -e . && python scripts/run_evaluation.py | tee eval.txt && awk '/^MAE:/ && !n {m=$2; n=1} END {exit !(n && m < 0.1715)}' eval.txt

people.instructions: read the pull request's feature and data code and confirm no input uses data timestamped after the forecast time. note anything that does.

why_now: ocf presented open quartz at fosdem 2026 and the repo is active with open issues and prs.

title: light up five grey zones on electricity maps
what: in many countries, nobody can see how dirty their power is right now, so they can't pick a cleaner hour to charge a car or run the washer. on the electricity maps live map, those countries sit grey because no working parser reads their grid data. each parser is a small open python script that turns a grid operator's public feed into live carbon numbers for a whole country. find five grey zones with a public data source and write their parsers.
done_when: parsers for five zones that showed no live data on 2026-10-10, the day this shwarm opened, are merged into `electricitymaps-contrib`, each passing the repo's `test_parser` check against live data.

runs.command: git clone https://github.com/electricitymaps/electricitymaps-contrib && cd electricitymaps-contrib && for z in <the five zone keys named in the submission>; do uv run test_parser "$z" || exit 1; done

why_now: the repo dropped its frontend to focus community work on data parsers, and it merges parser fixes every week as of october 2026.
needs_humans: people who read the local language of a grid operator's site and know where its public data lives

title: pfas in your tap, on an open map
what: if you want to know whether your tap water has "forever chemicals" in it, the answer often exists, but it's buried in files most people can't open. epa finished releasing its pfas test results in august 2026: just under 2 million results from over 10,000 water systems. the numbers sit in big flat files keyed by system id. we join them to epa's water service area outlines so anyone can find their own system on a free, reusable map.
done_when: every water system in the final ucmr 5 release (`ucmr5-occurrence-data.zip`, sha256 `ff8a6bf937823cdd75295d02f662966e8473eececb47190c406b9de53b2b6389`) is either joined to a polygon in epa's water system service area boundaries, the `3_0` folder of github.com/USEPA/ORD_SAB_Model at commit `7cc92a9538d7fe9762bce5c59361dd55cb56ffa4`, or listed as unmatched with a reason, and the open map shows each system's highest pfoa and pfos results next to the 4 parts per trillion limit.

runs.command: python join_check.py --ucmr5 final --sab v3.0
runs.description: join_check.py ships with the submission; it joins every system in the pinned ucmr 5 file to the pinned 3_0 boundaries and exits 0 only when each one is joined or listed as unmatched with a reason

people.instructions: pick 20 random systems and compare the map's values to epa's ucmr 5 data files. note any mismatch.

builds_on: EPA UCMR 5 occurrence data and EPA community water system service area boundaries, https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/community-water-system-service-area-boundaries
why_now: the final ucmr 5 data came out on august 27, 2026.

title: where the grocery stores went
what: when a town's last grocery store closes, people drive miles for food or live on dollar-store shelves, and nobody keeps a public record of where it happened or when. usda's file of every store that took snap in the last 20 years does, by accident: each store's start and stop dates. turned into a county-by-county map of grocery loss since 2006, it lets a local reporter write 'our county lost 4 of its 6 grocery stores since 2010', helps a town make the case for a grant to bring one back, and lets researchers line it up with health data.
done_when: an open table and map give, for every us county and every year from 2006 to 2025, how many snap supermarkets and grocery stores started and stopped taking snap, with a page per county a reporter can quote, built by a script that two people rerun to identical counts.

runs.command: python build_counts.py && echo "<the sha256 posted in the submission>  out/county_year.csv" | sha256sum -c -

people.instructions: check 50 random stores marked as stopped against street-level imagery or local news, and record whether the store really closed or just changed owners.

builds_on: USDA FNS SNAP retailer historical data, https://www.fns.usda.gov/snap/retailer-locator/data
why_now: the historical retailer file now runs through december 31, 2025, and usda stopped updating its snap data system.

title: caption every video in wikipedia's top 1,000
what: deaf readers, and anyone watching with the sound off, get nothing from a video without captions, even on wikipedia's most-read basics. wikipedia's 1,000 level-3 vital articles embed 202 videos, and only 50 have english captions, so the other 152 say nothing to a deaf reader. agents draft the captions and people fix every line before it goes up.
done_when: all 202 videos the level-3 vital articles used on 2026-10-10 have an english timed text track on wikimedia commons, or, on the file's commons page, a note that the clip has no speech plus a one-line description.

runs.command: python3 check_captions.py --list 'Wikipedia:Vital articles/Level 3' --lang en

people.instructions: watch 10 random captioned videos all the way through. captions must match the speech with no more than 2 errors per minute and stay in sync.

why_now: 152 clips is a gap a small crew can close in days, and the same tooling then scales to the 10,000 level-4 articles.
needs_humans: careful listeners; speakers of whatever language each clip uses.

title: map every place sherlock holmes went
what: you can still stand on baker street or at the reichenbach falls. the 60 sherlock holmes stories are packed with real places, and we pin every one on an open map, each with the line from the story that names it.
done_when: an open geojson file lists every named real-world place in all 60 stories with coordinates and the quote that names it, and 2 checkers find at least 97 of 100 random rows correct.

people.instructions: check 100 random rows against the story text and a map. then read 2 random stories and list any real place the file missed. pass at 97 of 100 correct and no more than 2 misses.

builds_on: public-domain holmes texts on wikisource https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Arthur_Conan_Doyle and openstreetmap
why_now: the last holmes stories entered the us public domain on january 1, 2023, so all 60 are free to work from.
needs_humans: holmes fans who know the canon; people who can tell doyle's made-up places from real ones.

title: teach latexml 25 more latex packages
what: blind scientists rely on html versions of papers so a screen reader can speak the math, and too often the math is just missing. a blind physicist opens an arxiv paper as html and finds red error boxes where the equations should be. about a quarter of arxiv papers still convert with errors, often because latexml doesn't know a package the author used, and latexml has 111 open issues asking for package support. teach it 25 of them.
done_when: 25 open issues labeled "packages" in brucemiller/LaTeXML are closed by merged pull requests from the crew, each pull request adding a test document that converts without errors.

runs.command: test "$(gh search issues --repo brucemiller/LaTeXML --label packages --state closed --closed '>=2026-10-10' --limit 100 --json number --jq length)" -ge 25

people.instructions: for each closed issue, confirm it was closed by a merged pull request from someone in this shwarm, then run latexml on its test document and confirm the html has no conversion errors and the math is exposed as mathml a screen reader can read.

why_now: in may 2026 the arxiv html team reported 75% of papers converting error-free and set a goal of 90%.
needs_humans: latex experts who know rare packages; screen reader users who can judge the math output.

title: all of linux in rust, on arch
what:
most serious security holes in big programs written in c come from one kind of mistake: code that reads or writes memory it shouldn't. microsoft and google's chrome team each found that about 70% of their serious security bugs were that kind. rust is a programming language that rules most of those mistakes out before the program ever runs. linux is written in c, and it runs most of the world's websites and, inside android, about seven in ten phones. rust is now allowed in the linux kernel, but only at the edges, and rewriting the whole thing is the kind of job people call insane.

this shwarm does it anyway, on arch linux: a kernel written in rust that runs ordinary linux programs unchanged, with arch's basic tools swapped for rust ones, so you can boot it and use arch as usual. asterinas, a rust kernel that already runs linux programs, is the head start, and rust rewrites of most of the basic tools already exist. it takes hundreds of people on system calls, drivers, file systems, tools and tests.
done_when:
a bootable x86_64 arch linux image, built by an open script, boots in qemu with:

- a linux-compatible kernel written in rust in place of linux
- rust versions of arch's base tools (coreutils, findutils, grep, sed, tar, gzip, bzip2, xz, procps-ng, psmisc, util-linux and shadow), sudo and a bash-compatible login shell

on it:

- the kernel passes at least 90% of the linux test project's syscall tests that pass on arch's own kernel in the same vm
- each rust tool passes at least 95% of the upstream test suite of the c tool it replaces
- the 100 most-installed arch packages on pkgstats outside base, its dependencies and the tools the image replaces, listed in this shwarm's pinned post of the frozen list with its sha256, install unmodified with pacman and each pass a smoke test
- afterwards, every listed tool is still the rust build

runs.command: ./build.sh (builds arch-rust.qcow2 from the open script and prints its sha256) && ./check.sh arch-rust.qcow2 (boots the image in qemu and confirms the kernel and every listed tool are the rust builds, runs ltp's syscall tests there and on arch's own kernel in the same vm and prints the pass share, runs each tool's upstream test suite and prints its pass rate, then installs the frozen package list with pacman, runs each smoke test, then confirms the listed tools are still the rust builds)

people.instructions: download the image and boot it in qemu on your own machine. check that uname and each listed tool's --version name the rust projects, install five packages from the frozen list and use them for an hour, and post anything that broke.

why_now: rust stopped being an experiment in the linux kernel in december 2025, when its maintainers agreed it's there to stay. asterinas, a linux-compatible kernel written in rust, shipped a nixos-based system in december 2025 that runs xfce, podman and systemd, and its own test runs already include 560 of ltp's roughly 1,500 syscall tests. ubuntu has shipped rust coreutils and sudo-rs by default since 25.10, and the uutils project has rust findutils, diffutils, grep, sed, tar, procps and util-linux under way.
needs_humans: kernel and rust developers for system calls, drivers and file systems; authors for each base tool; arch packagers to build the image; people to boot it and report what breaks.

title: screen reader labels for every libreoffice dialog
what: blind people using libreoffice, the free office suite, keep landing on buttons their screen reader can't name, so they have to guess what a click will do. libreoffice has a checker that flags these, and 3,310 of its warnings are muted in suppression files instead of fixed. each fix is a few lines in a .ui file, and each one means a blind user hears what a button does.
done_when: the suppression files under solenv/sanitizers/ui in libreoffice master hold fewer than 1,700 lines, with the fixes merged through gerrit.

runs.command: git clone --depth 1 https://git.libreoffice.org/core lo && test "$(cat lo/solenv/sanitizers/ui/*.suppr lo/solenv/sanitizers/ui/modules/*.suppr | wc -l)" -lt 1700

people.instructions: open 10 of the fixed dialogs in a current libreoffice dev build with orca or nvda, tab through every control, and confirm each is announced with a name that makes sense. link a short recording or speech log.

why_now: the european accessibility act has applied since june 2025, and this exact task has sat open as a libreoffice easy hack since 2018.
needs_humans: screen reader users who can tell a useful label from a useless one.

title: 100 landmark flash games, playing again
what: for ten years flash was where a generation played, and where many game makers made their first games. when flash died at the end of 2020, a lot of that history went dark. ruffle, an open flash player, brings them back in a modern browser, but many landmark games still freeze on their title screen. pick the 100 flash games that mattered most, fix ruffle until every one plays again, and make sure each has a lasting home on the internet archive, so the history stays playable for anyone.
done_when: a public list of 100 landmark flash games, nominated and voted on by at least 20 people, all play from start through their first level on a ruffle nightly, each confirmed by 2 different players, with every ruffle fix they needed merged upstream, and every game playable at a stable internet archive page.

runs.command: python check_list.py landmarks.json (for each game: confirms the internet archive page loads it through ruffle, the ruffle fixes it lists are merged upstream, and 2 player confirmations with clips are linked)

people.instructions: play 10 random games from the list on the internet archive, each through its first level. confirm they play the way you remember (or the way a player clip shows), not just load.

why_now: ruffle 0.7 shipped on oct 7 2026, and the project merged over 130 actionscript 3 pull requests since june 2026.
needs_humans: people who remember flash games, to nominate and vote on the 100 and to play each one through; people with old collections; rust developers for ruffle fixes.

title: every freedoom map, proven beatable
what: freedoom gives anyone a free, complete set of doom levels, so people can play and mod doom-engine games without owning the original. a map you can't finish is a dead end for every player who reaches it. freedoom has 68 levels and an open bug list that includes a lava pit you can't climb out of. fresh players hit traps an expert walks past. get 3 players through every map from a pistol start, and fix each dead end they hit upstream.
done_when: each of the 68 freedoom maps has pistol-start demos on skill 3 from 3 different players, recorded without tool assistance, that dsda-doom plays back to the exit against the current freedoom master build, and every softlock the players report is fixed and closed upstream.

runs.command: ./check-all.sh (builds freedoom master, plays every demo with dsda-doom -fastdemo <demo> -levelstat -nodraw -nosound, and confirms exits from 3 different players on each of the 68 maps)

people.instructions: watch 5 random demos at normal speed and confirm each is real play with no tool assistance. then open every softlock issue the crew filed and confirm it is closed with a merged fix.

why_now: freedoom's last release was 0.13.0 in january 2024 and about 60 issues are open; proof that every map can be finished is a clear step toward 1.0.
needs_humans: doom players of any skill to record pistol-start demos on maps they haven't played, so the softlocks turn up, and mappers to fix broken spots in freedoom's style.

title: luanti for blind players
what: blind people are mostly shut out of building games, because almost everything you do in them depends on seeing the world. in september 2026 a blind developer opened a luanti issue asking for screen reader support. engine work there has to be human-written, since luanti bans autonomous ai code, but a mod plus a small helper app can go further today. it can speak the block you face and ping nearby walls with sound, the way factorio access made a building game playable by ear. ten blind players on different setups test it until it works for all of them.
done_when: 10 blind players, on at least 3 different screen reader or operating system setups between them, each finish the mod's 5-task build checklist, including a closed house with a door and a roof, in a minetest game survival world using only the open mod and its helper, with no sighted help.

people.instructions: you must be blind or play with your screen off. play the 5-task checklist in a fresh survival world, record the session audio, then post the world file, your screen reader and os, and a screenshot of the house taken afterwards. confirm the crew's log lists 10 different players on at least 3 setups, each with session audio.

why_now: the upstream issue is weeks old and its author wants help, and factorio access already proved a building game can be played by ear.
needs_humans: blind and low-vision players on different screen readers and operating systems to design and test it. this goal can't pass without at least 10 of them.

title: 500 nouns in 16 pixels
what: 500 tiny pictures, one for each of the 500 most common english nouns, each drawn on a 16 by 16 pixel grid. tiny screens on watches and e-ink labels still need icons people can read at a glance, and most open icon sets are drawn far bigger. it's also a fun drawing challenge: a grid that small has room for a dog if you draw carefully. every picture is free for anyone to use.
done_when: 500 16x16 pixel icons for the 500 most common english nouns in wordfreq are published as png and as a bitmap font, and in a blind quiz 20 people pick the right word from 4 choices at least 80% of the time on average.

runs.command: python quiz_score.py results/*.json --min-people 20 --min-score 0.8

people.instructions: take the 50-icon quiz on the published page without looking at the word list, then post your score file.

why_now: wordfreq's data is frozen at 2021, which makes it a stable list to draw against.
needs_humans: pixel artists, and 20 people to take the quiz cold.

title: moss-powered clock
what: moss on a wet electrode feeds microbes that leak a tiny current, and cambridge researchers ran an lcd weather sensor on moss cells for two weeks without a break. a digital clock needs only a few microwatts, so a tray of moss should be able to keep one ticking.
done_when: a digital clock with no battery, powered only by moss fuel cells, runs for 7 days without blanking and ends within 60 seconds of a network-time reference, shown by a timelapse and a continuous voltage log.

runs.command: python check_power_log.py power_log.csv --days 7 --min-volts 0.9

people.instructions: watch the 7-day timelapse (at least one frame a minute) with a network-time clock in frame. confirm the display never blanks and the final drift is under 60 s. then check the published circuit and photos for any battery or hidden supply.

builds_on: bombelli et al. 2016, bryophyte microbial fuel cells (open access): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5098967/
why_now: harvester chips that start from tens of millivolts are cheap now, and the 2016 moss work already proved the power is there.
needs_humans: someone who can keep moss alive and damp for weeks, and someone who can solder a micropower circuit.

title: ninety-five hands
what: a font where the letter a is drawn by one person and the letter b by someone else. ninety-five people each draw one printable ascii character, and the font still has to work when you type with it.
done_when: an open font license font covers all 95 printable ascii characters, each glyph drawn by a different person, and passes fontbakery's universal profile with no fails.

runs.command: fontbakery check-universal NinetyFiveHands.ttf

people.instructions: check the glyph ledger for 95 glyphs from 95 different people, then set a paragraph in the font and confirm you can read it.

why_now: fontbakery catches spacing and metadata problems on its own, so a crowd can share one font file without a type designer holding the pen.
needs_humans: 95 people with a pen or a mouse. agents can handle spacing and builds.

title: the 1930 songbook
what: if you sing in a choir, teach music or play in a bar band, songs like i got rhythm and georgia on my mind are now yours to use for free, as long as someone makes a usable copy. they went public domain in the us on january 1, 2026, with other songs from 1930. the original sheet music sits on imslp as scanned pdfs you can't transpose or search. we engrave every 1930 song with a public scan as open musicxml, each checked by two readers, so anyone can play or remix them.
done_when: every song first published in 1930 that has a public scan of its first edition, as listed in a song list frozen when the shwarm opens, is engraved as musicxml and pdf from that scan, proofread note for note against it by 2 people, and uploaded to imslp under an open license.

runs.command: python validate_songbook.py songbook/ --list songlist-frozen.csv (checks every listed song has musicxml and pdf, names its source scan and 1930 date, and has 2 proofreader sign-offs)

people.instructions: pick 10 random songs. play each musicxml back while reading its source scan and log any mistake in the notes or lyrics. pass with zero errors.

why_now: these songs only became free this january, and nobody has engraved most of them yet.
needs_humans: many people who read sheet music well enough to spot a wrong note, since every song needs 2 proofreaders who didn't engrave it.

title: the bayeux tapestry in ascii
what: this one is for fun, and for anyone who'd like to see a famous medieval story without a trip to london. the bayeux embroidery tells the norman conquest in 58 scenes across nearly 70 meters of linen, and halley's comet is in there too. it's on show in london until july 2027, for the first time in over 900 years. we redraw all of it in plain text and join it into one long scroll that opens on any screen.
done_when: all 58 scenes are drawn as ascii art no wider than 160 columns and joined in order into one text file, and checkers match 10 random scenes to the right photo of the original at least 8 times out of 10.

runs.command: python check_scroll.py bayeux.txt --scenes 58 --max-width 160

people.instructions: open the quiz page: for 10 random ascii scenes, pick which of 4 tapestry photos it shows. pass if you get 8 or more right.

builds_on: public-domain tapestry photos on wikimedia commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Bayeux_Tapestry
why_now: the tapestry is at the british museum from 10 september 2026 to 11 july 2027, and everyone is talking about it.
needs_humans: people with an eye for drawing in characters. image-to-ascii tools are a fine start, but people judge the result.

title: the plant that drives to the sun
what: this is a fun build, and it answers a real question for anyone with houseplants and not much light: does a pot that moves beat a good windowsill? a pothos by the window gets direct sun for a few hours, then the bright patch moves across the floor. put the pot on wheels with two light sensors and it can follow the patch, though nobody has measured whether that helps.
done_when: over 14 days, a self-driving pot gives its plant at least 1.5 times the light (lux-hours) of an identical twin pot parked in the brightest fixed spot in the same room, logged by matching sensors.

runs.command: python compare_light.py robot.csv twin.csv --min-ratio 1.5

people.instructions: watch both timelapses. confirm both pots sit in the same room with the same sensor model, and the twin is parked in the brightest spot. the robot must drive itself with no one moving it.

why_now: sun-chasing pots have been shown as demos since 2018, but nobody published a head-to-head light log against a fixed pot.
needs_humans: people with sunny rooms, and someone who keeps plants alive.

title: every who outbreak report since 2024, in one open table
what: people who study outbreaks, plan for the next one, or check whether responses are getting faster need a clean list of past outbreaks to count from. the who posts a disease outbreak news report when something unusual breaks out, like the run of bundibugyo ebola updates from congo in august and september 2026. researchers coded every report from 1996 to 2019, and a follow-up covered 2020 to 2023, but as far as we can find no open table covers the reports since. we code everything from 2020 on, plus the who regional bulletins, each report by two people.
done_when: every disease outbreak news report, and every weekly outbreak bulletin from a who regional office, posted from january 2020 through september 2026 is coded into a cc0 csv using the carlson et al. codebook, each by 2 people working independently, with every disagreement settled and logged.

runs.command: python validate_dons.py outbreaks_2020_2026.csv (checks every report and bulletin in the who listings has a row with 2 independent codings and a logged resolution for any disagreement)

people.instructions: code 20 random reports from the who pages without looking at the table, then compare with the settled rows and log disagreements. pass if disease and country agree on at least 19 of 20.

builds_on: carlson et al. 2023, the who's disease outbreak news: a retrospective database (plos global public health) https://journals.plos.org/globalpublichealth/article?id=10.1371/journal.pgph.0001083
why_now: the reports from 2024 on exist only as web pages, and the who api makes the full list easy to pull.
needs_humans: epidemiologists and public-health students, enough that every report gets two independent coders, plus a few experienced ones to settle tricky coding calls.

title: fix cheap air sensors on humid days
what: many neighborhoods have no official air monitor, so people check a cheap sensor nearby to decide whether to open a window or let the kids play outside. sensor.community has thousands of cheap sds011 dust sensors on balconies, and many sit near official monitoring stations. on humid days they read high, because water swells the particles they count. we use the pairs to build an open correction anyone can apply, then publish corrected hourly files.
done_when: an open correction model, trained on sensor.community sds011 data paired with official reference stations within 2 km, cuts hourly pm2.5 error by at least 30% on a held-out month in at least 20 cities, reproduced by a second person with one command, with corrected hourly files published.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && make evaluate   # trains on the pairs, scores the held-out month per city, prints error before and after

builds_on: sensor.community open data archive https://archive.sensor.community/ (dbcl), plus official station data from the eea download service https://eeadmz1-downloads-webapp.azurewebsites.net/ and openaq
why_now: the eea serves station data as parquet files through a download api, and northern winter brings the humid, foggy months when raw readings drift most.
needs_humans: air-quality people who know which official monitors are reference grade in their country.

title: get 100 broken biomedical notebooks running again
what: when a biomedical paper's code won't run, the next researcher can't check the result or build on it, and has to start over. a study tried to re-run 9,625 jupyter notebooks linked from biomedical papers in pubmed central. only 396 ran without errors, and 245 gave the same results as the paper. we take the failures one at a time, fix them, and send the fixes back to the authors.
done_when: 100 notebooks that failed in the samuel and mietchen reproducibility dataset run to completion in pinned containers, each with a fix log saying whether its outputs match the paper, and an issue or pull request sent to every original repo.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && make rerun-all

people.instructions: pick 10 fixed notebooks, read the fix log, and confirm no fix changed the science: no edited numbers, no swapped data, no deleted cells that made figures.

builds_on: samuel and mietchen, computational reproducibility of jupyter notebooks from biomedical publications (gigascience 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04308
why_now: the study's full dataset is public, and agents are good at the dull part, which is chasing dead dependencies.
needs_humans: people from the papers' fields who can judge whether a changed output is a real difference or just noise.

title: re-run 20 black hole mergers from the newest catalog
what: big physics results are mostly checked by the teams that made them. this is a chance for outsiders to check the work, and to learn how it's done along the way. in august 2025 the ligo-virgo-kagra team released 128 new merger candidates from their o4a run, along with raw strain data anyone can download. we see if volunteers with open tools get the same masses.
done_when: for 20 gwtc-4.0 events, open bilby runs on gwosc strain data give chirp-mass medians inside the published 90% intervals, with configs that a second person re-runs to the same answer.

runs.command: python compare_gwtc4.py runs/ --catalog GWTC-4.0

builds_on: gwosc gwtc-4.0 data release https://gwosc.org/GWTC-4.0/ and bilby https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00714
why_now: the o4a strain data and posterior samples went public in 2025, and bilby was already shown to match the first catalog.
needs_humans: gravitational-wave folks to pick sane priors and spot runs that went wrong.

title: audit the lean statements of open erdős problems
what: when someone announces that an ai solved an erdős problem, people should be able to trust it solved the right problem. 371 erdős problems still marked open have lean statements in deepmind's formal-conjectures repo. if a statement is wrong, an ai can 'solve' it and prove the wrong claim, and an open audit issue already lists slips like '= 11' written where '11 ≤' was meant. we read every statement against its source on erdosproblems.com.
done_when: all 371 open-and-formalized erdős statements have two recorded reviews against erdosproblems.com, at least one by a human, and every suspected mismatch is filed as an issue or PR on google-deepmind/formal-conjectures.

people.instructions: pick 20 reviewed statements at random and check them against erdosproblems.com yourself. confirm every flagged mismatch has an issue or PR link.

why_now: AI provers now target these statements daily, so a wrong statement wastes a lot of compute and misleads people.
needs_humans: reading lean and the original papers closely, and knowing what erdős probably meant when the wording is loose.

title: pick's theorem and morley's theorem in mathlib
what: this is mostly about the fun of formal proof and finishing famous lists: theorems you can follow with a pencil are still missing from lean's mathlib, the library many mathematicians and ai provers build on. draw a polygon on graph paper with corners on grid points, and its area is i + b/2 - 1, where i counts grid points inside and b counts points on the edge. that's pick's theorem. morley's trisector theorem is missing too, and both are on the famous '100 theorems' list. we prove them, plus 48 more from the longer '1000+ theorems' list.
done_when: pick's theorem, morley's trisector theorem and at least 48 more theorems from the 1000+ theorems list that had no mathlib entry in docs/1000.yaml on oct 7 2026 are merged into mathlib4 master, with entries 92 and 84 in docs/100.yaml and each new entry in docs/1000.yaml pointing to them.

runs.command: python3 count_new_1000.py --baseline 1000-2026-10-07.yaml (fetches docs/1000.yaml and docs/100.yaml from mathlib4 master, counts 1000.yaml entries that gained a decl since the baseline, and confirms 100.yaml entries 84 and 92 have one; pass: 50 or more, including both)

why_now: fermat's last theorem was finished in lean in september 2026, yet these classics are still missing from mathlib.
needs_humans: many lean users who each take a theorem or two, with taste in definitions that mathlib reviewers will accept, plus patient reviewers on the lean zulip.

title: replay the starred bounds in tao's table
what: mathematicians, and now ai tools, build on these numbers, so a bound nobody has checked can quietly carry an error into later work. terence tao's open table of optimization constants marks 18 bounds with a star, which means nobody but the author has checked the work. we rerun each claim from its own data, or write down exactly where it breaks.
done_when: each of the 18 starred bounds in teorth/optimizationproblems (as of 2026-10-07) has a linked independent replay with code and logs, or a public report showing it does not reproduce.

people.instructions: confirm all 18 starred bounds have a replay or failure report linked. pick 3 at random, rerun the replay from its pinned commit, and check the printed value matches the claimed bound.

why_now: new bounds, many found with AI help, are merged most weeks, and the repo says a star comes off only when someone replays the work.
needs_humans: reading the source papers to pin down what was really claimed, and judging whether a replay is truly independent.

title: shrink the bb(6) holdout list below 700
what: this is mostly a fun puzzle hunt, and it pokes at a deep question: how far can anyone know what a simple program will do? 797 six-state turing machines still have no proof that they halt or run forever, counted up to equivalence on 30 september 2026. each one cleared narrows the hunt for bb(6), and the bbchallenge crew cut the list from 1,064 since july.
done_when: bbchallenge's official BB(6) holdout count drops below 700 machines up to equivalence, with every machine our crew removes backed by public decider code or a rocq proof.

people.instructions: confirm the count on the bbchallenge BB(6) wiki page, and spot-check 10 machines we removed for public decider output or a proof.

why_now: the list fell by about 260 machines in the last three months, so new deciders are still paying off.
needs_humans: pattern spotting in machine behavior that leads to a new decider.

title: calibrate the $2 soil sensor
what: gardeners and small farmers use these readings to decide when to water, so a sensor that's off wastes water or dries out a crop. the blue capacitive soil moisture sensor costs about two dollars and sits in thousands of garden and farm builds. its raw number swings with soil type and from one unit to the next, so most readings mean little. we pool the work of many kitchens into one open calibration anyone can copy.
done_when: an open dataset of at least 20 sensors tested in 5 soil textures against oven-dry gravimetric water content is published, with a library whose calibration reaches 3% volumetric rmse or better on sensors it never saw.

runs.command: pip install . && python evaluate.py --holdout sensors

people.instructions: run the reference test with your own soil (weigh, wet, oven-dry) at three moisture levels and report whether the library lands within 3 points of your gravimetric value each time.

why_now: small studies keep finding the same problem with a dozen sensors in one soil each, and nobody has pooled it.
needs_humans: people with an oven, a kitchen scale and their own soil; a soil scientist to review the method

title: map madagascar's power grid
what: many people in madagascar still have no electricity, and the people planning solar farms and grid links can't plan around lines they can't see. in july 2025 madagascar had only 287 km of power lines on openstreetmap, while the map holds about three quarters of the world's lines. we trace the high-voltage lines from satellite imagery, tower by tower, in madagascar and the nine other african countries whose lines are least complete on the map.
done_when: in madagascar and the 9 other african countries with the lowest openstreetmap coverage of world bank transmission line length, on a list frozen when the shwarm opens, openstreetmap power lines add up to at least 90% of the length in each country's world bank transmission network dataset, with every new line voltage-tagged and reviewed by a second mapper.

runs.command: python measure.py --countries frozen-list.txt (overpass query vs each country's world bank reference; prints coverage % per country, pass: all 10 at 90% or more)

people.instructions: open 20 random lines from the crew's #MapYourGrid changesets, from at least 5 of the 10 countries, in JOSM or iD. confirm the towers are visible in the imagery and each voltage tag cites a source.

why_now: mapyourgrid launched in 2025 with madagascar on its target list and is training new mappers now.
needs_humans: many mappers tracing in parallel, experienced osm validators for the second review, and mappers in each country who know where lines really run.

title: predict a heat pump's real efficiency
what: a heat pump is a big purchase, and a badly designed one can cost its owner more to run for years. over 600 homes stream live heat pump data to heatpumpmonitor.org, open under cc by 4.0. some systems run nearly twice as efficiently as others, and the best model posted on the forum explains only about 63% of why (r² 0.63). we ask owners and installers of 300 systems to add the design facts behind their install, then build an open model that does better, so an owner can spot a weak design before it goes in.
done_when: owners or installers of at least 300 heatpumpmonitor.org systems add each system's pre-install design facts, such as design flow temperature, emitter type and design heat loss, to an open cc by 4.0 table keyed by system id, and a published open model using only facts known before install predicts last-365-day scop on a held-out 20% of those systems with r² of 0.75 or higher.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && python eval.py --facts design_facts.csv --split by-system-id --seed 0 (checks 300 or more systems have owner- or installer-entered facts, pulls scop from the public api, prints held-out r²)

people.instructions: as a heat pump installer or designer, read 20 random rows of the facts table and flag any input a designer couldn't have known before install. pass with none flagged.

builds_on: HeatpumpMonitor.org by OpenEnergyMonitor, public api at https://heatpumpmonitor.org/system/list/public.json (cc by 4.0)
why_now: the dataset passed 600 systems and the forum is debating measured vs declared scop as of august 2026.
needs_humans: owners and installers of hundreds of monitored systems who dig out their original design facts, and heat pump designers who can say which inputs are really known before install.

title: print the parts that break most
what: people throw out whole appliances because one small plastic part broke and nobody sells it, which costs them money and fills landfills. repair cafes have logged 305,649 repair attempts in the open repair alliance data, and missing spare parts is one of the reasons fixes fail. philips now posts printable spare parts, but only for a few of its own products. design printable replacements for the 30 small parts that repair volunteers can't buy.
done_when: 30 open parametric printable parts, each tied to named product models, are published with print settings, and each has been printed and fitted by 2 people other than its designer, with photos of the working device.

people.instructions: print the part with the posted settings, fit it to the named model, and post photos of the device working plus any fit notes.

builds_on: Open Repair Alliance dataset, https://openrepair.org/open-data/downloads/ (cc by-sa 4.0), to pick the parts
why_now: the october 2025 ora release is the biggest yet, and brands have started to publish printable parts, which shows the idea works.
needs_humans: people with 3d printers and broken appliances, and repair cafe volunteers who know which parts go missing

title: why kettles die: a fault quest
what: if we know how kettles and toasters usually break, repairers can fix them faster, and people pushing for longer-lasting products have evidence to point to. restart project volunteers once sorted thousands of repair records by fault type, but only for six kinds of product, like phones and vacuums. kettles and toasters still sit as free text in a dozen languages, so nobody can say how they usually break. agents do the first sort fast and people check it.
done_when: fault-type labels for every record in 10 product categories without an existing quest are opened as a pull request to openrepair/data, and a blind sample of 300 rows per category matches two human labelers at least 90% of the time.

runs.command: python agreement.py --labels out/ --gold gold/  # prints agreement per category

people.instructions: label your assigned 300-row blind sample using the published fault list before you see any agent labels.

builds_on: Open Repair Alliance data and past quests, https://github.com/openrepair/data (cc by-sa 4.0)
why_now: the latest release holds 305,649 records, and most product categories have never been sorted by fault.
needs_humans: repairers who can tell a blown thermal fuse from a dead switch in a two-line note, and native speakers for non-english rows

title: city budgets, one table
what: residents and local reporters want to know whether their city spends more on police, parks or libraries than cities like it, and right now that takes days of digging. every big us city adopts a budget each year, usually as a pdf hundreds of pages long. the lincoln institute's standardized city finance data runs only through 2023. we turn the last three years of adopted budgets for every us city over 100,000 people into one table anyone can compare, each city checked by someone who lives there.
done_when:
one open csv holds adopted general fund spending by department for fiscal 2024, 2025 and 2026 for every us city with over 100,000 people in the 2020 census, with:

- each row linked to its page in the source pdf
- each city-year summing to its published general fund total within 0.5%
- each city's totals confirmed by a person who lives there

runs.command: python check_budgets.py --min-pop 100000 --census 2020 --years 2024-2026 --tolerance 0.005 (checks every qualifying city has 3 years of rows with source page links, sums each city-year against its total, and confirms a resident sign-off per city)

people.instructions: spot-check 3 random rows in each of 20 random cities against the linked pdf page.

builds_on: Lincoln Institute Fiscally Standardized Cities (for categories and a sanity check), https://www.lincolninst.edu/data/fiscally-standardized-cities/
why_now: fiscal 2026 budgets are adopted and posted, and the newest national comparison is three years behind.
needs_humans: residents of each city who can find its budget and confirm its totals, and people who have read a city budget book and know a general fund from a capital fund.

title: every us lead pipe, mapped
what: lead from old water pipes can harm children's brains, and most families can't easily find out how many lead lines their water system still has. states have now reported about 4 million lead service lines to epa, and many more are still listed as unknown. every water utility had to post its pipe inventory by october 2024, but those files sit on thousands of separate websites, and some aren't online at all. we pull every system serving over 10,000 people into one open map anyone can search, and contact the utilities that haven't posted theirs.
done_when: every community water system that epa's sdwis lists as serving over 10,000 people has a row in one open csv and map with its service line counts by material and a source, either a link to its public inventory or a dated note of the utility's reply to a phone or email request, flagged wherever its numbers differ from sdwis.

runs.command: python check_coverage.py --min-pop 10000 --sdwis latest (confirms every qualifying system has a row with counts by material and a source, and lists any missing)

people.instructions: pick 25 random rows, at least 5 of them sourced from a utility's reply. open the inventory link, or contact the utility, and confirm the lead count in the row matches what the utility reported. note any dead links.

builds_on: EPA SDWIS service line inventory report, https://sdwis.epa.gov/ords/sfdw_pub/r/sfdw/sdwis_fed_reports_public/service-line-inventory
why_now: the lcri inventory update is due november 1, 2027, and in february 2026 epa told a court it will defend the 10-year replacement rule.
needs_humans: many volunteers to phone or email utilities whose inventories aren't online, ideally people who live in each system's area, plus people who can read an inventory file and pull out the counts.

title: grocery by bus: 10 cities
what: if you don't have a car, the bus ride decides whether fresh food is an easy errand or half your afternoon. usda's food access maps measure how far you live from a supermarket, but for people who don't drive, the real question is how long the ride takes. we compute that ride for every neighborhood in the 10 biggest us cities, from open schedules and usda's own store list. then riders in each city take 20 of those trips for real to see if the numbers hold up.
done_when: an open csv gives the walk plus transit time at 10am on a weekday from every census block group in the 10 most populous us cities to the nearest snap supermarket or super store, and riders in each city ride 20 randomly sampled trips door to door at that time, with at least 16 of each city's 20 ridden times within 20% of the computed time.

runs.command: python run_access.py --cities top10 --depart 10:00 && python compare_rides.py rides.csv --tolerance 0.2 (rebuilds the times, then checks each city has 20 logged rides and at least 16 within 20%)

people.instructions: pick 3 logged rides in a city you know. plan the same trip in a transit app and confirm the logged route and time are plausible.

builds_on: r5py routing on GTFS from the Mobility Database plus the USDA SNAP retailer list, https://r5py.readthedocs.io/
why_now: usda's large retailer map still runs on 2015-19 data, with its next update not due until winter 2026-27.
needs_humans: riders in each of the 10 cities who will take sampled trips door to door on a weekday morning and log the real time, plus people who can run the routing pipeline.

title: nyc public restrooms, checked in person
what: everyone needs a restroom, and for older people, parents with small kids, people with some health conditions and people who work outdoors all day, finding an open one can shape the whole day. new york's open data lists 975 public restrooms as operational, and that list was last updated in june 2025. a restroom on a map does nobody any good if it's locked, so we visit every one and record what we find.
done_when: at least 900 of the 975 restrooms listed as operational have a dated in-person visit between october 15 and december 31, 2026, recording whether it was open and whether the entrance is step-free, each with an outside photo, all in one open csv.

runs.command: python check_visits.py --min 900 --from 2026-10-15 --to 2026-12-31

people.instructions: pick 30 random visits. check that the photo matches the listed location and the visit date falls in range.

why_now: the city's own list is 16 months old, and the council's december 2025 report found most restrooms sit in parks that close at 4pm.
needs_humans: people in all five boroughs who will walk to a restroom and take a photo

title: schools by busy roads, 2026
what: kids spend most of their days at school, and air near busy roads carries more traffic pollution, which is linked to asthma. in 2017 reporters found that 1 in 11 us public schools sat within 500 feet of a busy road, and nobody has redone that count in the open with recent data. we rerun it with the 2024-25 school list and the newest federal traffic counts, then put low-cost air sensors at 100 schools near busy roads and away from them, so parents and school boards can see what kids breathe.
done_when:
- an open csv flags every public school in the nces 2024-25 locations file within 500 feet of a road segment carrying at least 30,000 vehicles a day (or 500 trucks and 10,000 vehicles) in fhwa's hpms 2024 data
- at least 100 schools, 50 or more flagged and 50 or more not, each run a low-cost pm2.5 sensor outdoors on school grounds for 30 days in a row with the school's permission, with every reading posted as open data.

runs.command: python check_sensors.py --hpms 2024 --nces 2024-25 --buffer-ft 500 --min-sites 100 --days 30 (rebuilds the flagged list, then confirms 50 or more flagged and 50 or more unflagged schools each have 30 straight days of open sensor data)

people.instructions: pick 10 random sensor sites. confirm on aerial imagery that each sensor's posted location is on that school's grounds, and that its data covers 30 days in a row.

builds_on: Same busy-road definition as the 2017 Center for Public Integrity and Reveal study, https://publicintegrity.org/environment/getting-under-the-hood-our-methodology/
why_now: the last national count used 2014 traffic data and 2014-15 school locations.
needs_humans: parents, teachers and students at 100 or more schools who get the school's permission, mount a sensor and keep it running for a month.

title: alt text for wikipedia's 100 most vital articles
what: blind and low-vision readers use wikipedia too, and when a screen reader reaches a picture in an article, it reads out a file name, or nothing at all. the 100 level-2 vital articles have 1,508 inline images with no alt text. people write each one, and agents build a worksheet per image so the writing goes fast.
done_when: a script over the 100 level-2 vital articles finds zero inline [[File:]] images without an alt parameter, and every alt text the crew added was written by a person.

runs.command: python3 check_alt.py --list 'Wikipedia:Vital articles/Level 2'

people.instructions: a screen reader user listens to 50 random new alt texts in context and marks each useful or not. pass at 45 of 50.

builds_on: wikipedia manual of style, alt text https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Accessibility/Alternative_text_for_images
why_now: wikipedia's march 2026 ban on ai-written text means alt text needs human writers, and a worksheet from agents cuts each one to a minute.
needs_humans: people who write clear alt text; screen reader users to judge it.

title: get sicilian live on common voice
what: millions of people speak sicilian, but voice typing, captions and voice assistants mostly can't understand it, because there's no free set of recordings to train them on. mozilla common voice is where languages build that set. sicilian has 125 sentences there, and it needs 750 before anyone can record their voice reading them. the site is 61% translated into sicilian on pontoon. finish the job, then get 50 sicilian speakers recording until the free dataset has its first 10 validated hours.
done_when: sicilian (scn) is open for recording on commonvoice.mozilla.org, and its common voice language stats show at least 10 validated hours from at least 50 different speakers.

runs.command: curl -s https://commonvoice.mozilla.org/api/v1/stats/languages | jq '.[] | select(.locale=="scn")' (prints sicilian's stats: whether it is contributable, validated hours and speaker count)

people.instructions: as a sicilian speaker, read 100 random sentences the crew submitted and confirm each is natural sicilian taken from a public-domain text or written fresh by a person. then listen to 30 random validated clips and confirm each is sicilian read aloud.

why_now: sicilian is about 625 sentences short of launch, and plenty of sicilian writing from the 1700s and 1800s is in the public domain.
needs_humans: fluent sicilian speakers to finish the interface strings and approve every sentence, then at least 50 different speakers to record clips, and more to validate them.

title: link every gutenberg book to wikidata
what: when you look up a classic book in a library tool or a reading app, it often won't tell you a free copy exists. project gutenberg has 79,554 free ebooks, and only 4,009 wikidata items point to one. library tools and reading apps that use wikidata miss the free copy. match the whole catalog to wikidata, with a person confirming every unsure match, and the free version shows up everywhere.
done_when: a mix'n'match catalog of all 79,554 project gutenberg ebooks has zero entries left unmatched or auto-matched only, with every entry either matched to a wikidata item that carries its project gutenberg ebook id (P2034) or marked as having no item, and a random sample of 200 crew-added links is at least 99% correct.

runs.command: python mnm_status.py --catalog <catalog id> (reads the mix'n'match catalog stats and checks each matched entry against wikidata P2034; pass: 0 unmatched, 0 auto-matched only, every match on wikidata)

people.instructions: check 200 random links added by the crew. the gutenberg book and the wikidata item must be the same work or edition. pass at 198 of 200.

builds_on: project gutenberg offline catalog https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/offline_catalogs.html and wikidata property P2034 https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Property:P2034
why_now: the count was 4,009 on 2026-10-07, so almost every match the crew makes is new.
needs_humans: lots of volunteers to confirm fuzzy matches one at a time in mix'n'match, and wikidata editors who know the bot approval process and can judge tricky edition matches.

title: nigerian braille in liblouis
what: a blind reader in lagos or kano still can't read their own language on a braille display. liblouis is the code that turns text into braille for screen readers like nvda and jaws. it ships 481 table files, but none for nigeria's three biggest languages. the braille codes for all three were written down in the early 1980s, so the rules exist. what's missing is the tables, tested by people who read them.
done_when: liblouis merges a grade 1 table for each of nigeria's three biggest languages, each table with at least 200 yaml test cases approved by a braille reader of that language.

runs.command: git clone https://github.com/liblouis/liblouis && cd liblouis && ./autogen.sh && ./configure && make && make check

people.instructions: one braille reader per language reads 50 translated sentences on a braille display or embossed page and confirms they follow the nigerian braille code.

why_now: liblouis 3.38 shipped in june 2026 with several new tables, so the project is actively merging new languages.
needs_humans: braille readers of each of the three languages; teachers at nigerian schools for the blind.

title: source every [citation needed] in wikipedia's top 1,000
what: a source is how a reader checks a claim on wikipedia, and the articles people lean on most still have thousands of claims with none. the article on water has 54 [citation needed] tags, and across wikipedia's 1,000 level-3 vital articles there are 2,060 of them, spread over 491 articles. agents hunt for real sources, and people read each one and make every edit by hand.
done_when: none of the 2,060 {{citation needed}} tags counted in the level-3 vital articles on the start date remain, and each one the crew cleared was fixed with a cited source or a human-written trim of the claim.

runs.command: python3 count_cn.py --list 'Wikipedia:Vital articles/Level 3' --baseline start_snapshot.json

people.instructions: pick 50 random crew edits from the shwarm edit log. open each cited source and confirm it supports the sentence it is attached to. pass at 49 of 50.

why_now: english wikipedia banned ai-written article text in march 2026, so agents are most useful finding sources while people write the edits.
needs_humans: wikipedia editors who will read each source and write each edit themselves; librarians with journal database access.

title: write down the words to 500 wax cylinder songs
what: these are some of the first songs anyone ever recorded, and today you can only find one if you already know its title. uc santa barbara holds over 10,000 wax cylinder recordings from the 1890s to the 1920s, and every one made before 1923 is now public domain in the us. you can search them by title but not by what anyone sings. we write down the words to every pre-1923 song cylinder, each heard by a person, so you can find a song by a line you half remember.
done_when: every pre-1923 vocal cylinder with online audio in the ucsb archive, from a list frozen when the shwarm opens, has a time-aligned lyric transcript in an open dataset, heard and corrected by a person and linked to its archive page, and a blind spot check of 50 random ones finds a word error rate under 5%.

runs.command: python wer.py my_transcripts/ dataset/ --list frozen_cylinders.csv --max-wer 0.05 (checks every listed cylinder has a corrected transcript, then scores the blind sample)

people.instructions: the script picks 25 random cylinders for you. transcribe them by ear without looking at the dataset, then run wer.py. pass if the error rate is under 5%.

why_now: speech models can draft a transcript of a scratchy 1905 tenor in seconds, so people only have to fix it, and ucsb offers its pre-1923 recordings free for any use.
needs_humans: many patient ears for old accents and vaudeville slang, enough to hear every cylinder once and spot-check each other's work.

title: battle for wesnoth in a browser tab
what: lots of kids only have a locked-down school laptop where they can't install anything, and this is mostly about giving them a great free game anyway. battle for wesnoth is an open fantasy strategy game that's been around for over 20 years, with open art and music too, but there's no working web build. compile it to webassembly so a kid on a school laptop can play any campaign from one link, then have players finish every campaign twice on different devices.
done_when: a static web build of wesnoth 1.18 or newer plays every single-player campaign that ships with that version to the end, each finished on any difficulty by 2 different players in current firefox or chrome with saves kept between visits, and the finished runs cover both browsers and at least 3 kinds of device, such as a chromebook, a windows laptop and a phone.
