people.instructions: play one campaign of your choice to the end in the hosted build. report crashes, whether saves survive a reload, your device and the frame rate. then confirm the crew's log shows 2 finishes by different players for every campaign, covering both browsers and at least 3 kinds of device.

why_now: wesnoth 1.20 is getting close (dev builds are at 1.19.28), and emscripten ships an sdl2 port that wesnoth's renderer can sit on.
needs_humans: lots of players who know wesnoth's campaigns, on different browsers and devices, to finish each one twice and spot when units or the computer opponent act wrong.

title: clear the arch wiki's out-of-date flags
what: the arch wiki is where a lot of linux users, not only arch users, go when something breaks, and stale steps there can make things worse. 312 arch wiki pages carry a box saying part of the page is out of date, and people land on them from search and follow the old steps anyway. test the steps on a fresh install, fix the page and take the box down.
done_when: the arch wiki category of pages flagged out of date holds 160 or fewer pages, each removed flag tied to an edit that says how it was tested, with none reverted after 14 days.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://wiki.archlinux.org/api.php?action=query&prop=categoryinfo&titles=Category:Pages_or_sections_flagged_with_Template:Out_of_date&format=json' | jq '.query.pages[].categoryinfo.pages'   # 312 on oct 7 2026; pass: 160 or lower

people.instructions: pick 10 fixed sections at random, follow the new steps on a fresh arch vm or spare machine, and report whether they work as written.

why_now: 312 is small enough to finish, and many of those pages have just one stale section.
needs_humans: arch users with real hardware a vm can't fake, like laptops and gpus.

title: every arch core package, rebuilt bit for bit
what: every time you install an update, you trust that the file you got was built from the code anyone can read. a package that rebuilds exactly is proof nobody slipped code in between the source and your machine. arch rebuilds its packages from source to check the result matches the file it ships, byte for byte. in the core repo, 280 pass and 9 still come out different, including grub and the lts kernel, and extra had 1,513 on oct 7 2026. we fix core and 500 in extra, each rebuilt by different people on their own machines.
done_when: reproducible.archlinux.org lists zero bad packages in core and at least 500 fewer bad packages in extra than the 1,513 listed on oct 7 2026, and every package fixed along the way rebuilds to the shipped checksum on 2 more machines run by 2 different people, each posting a signed run report.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://reproducible.archlinux.org/api/v0/pkgs/list?status=BAD' | jq '[.[] | select(.suite=="core")] | length, ([.[] | select(.suite=="extra")] | length)' (prints bad counts for core and extra; pass: 0, then 1013 or lower)

people.instructions: pick 5 packages from the crew's fixed list, rebuild each with archlinux-repro on your own machine, and confirm the checksum matches the shipped package. then confirm the crew's log has 2 independent rebuild reports from different people for every fixed package.

why_now: core is down to its last 9 holdouts, and the reproducible builds folks publish diffoscope output for each one, so you can see exactly what differs.
needs_humans: people with their own machines to run independent rebuilds, and packagers who can get fixes accepted upstream and in arch's packaging repos.

title: python's docs in bengali
what: plenty of people learning to code read english slowly or not at all, and python's official docs assume they read it well. more than 230 million people speak bengali, and python's official docs in bengali are at 0%. docs.python.org adds a language to its switcher once the tutorial plus two short pages are fully translated. we go past that to the built-in types page and 20 standard library pages, with two fluent readers checking every file.
done_when: translations.python.org shows bengali core at 100%, library/stdtypes and 20 more standard library module pages from a list fixed when the shwarm opens are fully translated, every translated file is reviewed by two native speakers, and a pull request adding bengali to the docs.python.org language switcher is merged.

runs.command: python check_po.py python-docs-bn-in/ --files core-and-listed.txt (counts translated and fuzzy entries in each listed .po file; pass: 100% translated, none fuzzy)

people.instructions: as a native bengali reader, read 3 random translated pages from the tutorial, stdtypes or the listed module pages next to the english and mark every error in meaning. pass if no page has more than 2. also confirm translations.python.org lists bengali core at 100%.

why_now: the official bengali repo exists under the python org but hasn't moved since may 2025, so it's waiting for a team.
needs_humans: many native bengali speakers who know some python, so every file gets two reviewers, and one person willing to be the translation coordinator python asks for.

title: tests for ffmpeg's untested filters
what: ffmpeg sits underneath a lot of the video and audio software people use every day, so a quiet bug in it can break many apps at once. its public coverage report shows 149 audio and video filter files where its test suite runs zero lines, including af_biquads, the code behind its equalizer. a small test for each, with its expected output checked by a second person against another tool, catches the next silent break before it ships to every app built on ffmpeg.
done_when: coverage.ffmpeg.org shows every one of the 149 software filter files that had 0% line coverage on oct 7 2026 at 50% or more through fate tests merged upstream, and each new test's reference output is checked by someone other than its author against an independent tool such as sox or imagemagick, or by ear or eye where no such tool exists.

runs.command: python3 untested_filters.py --baseline baseline-2026-10-07.txt (scrapes coverage.ffmpeg.org and counts baseline files now at 50% line coverage or more; pass: 149)

people.instructions: pick 5 random new fate tests. regenerate the reference output with the independent tool, or check it by ear or eye, and confirm it matches the test's reference and that the logged checker isn't the test's author.

why_now: ffmpeg now takes pull requests on its own forgejo, which makes small test patches much easier to send.
needs_humans: audio and video people who can tell whether a filter's output is right, enough of them that every test gets a checker who didn't write it.

title: a game boy game on a real cartridge
what: an epic new game boy game, released on a real, physical cartridge you can hold in your hands and play on a 1989 game boy. this one is for fun. gb studio lets anyone make a real game boy game without writing assembly, and a crowd can finish what solo makers often drop: a full adventure with its own art and music that boots on original hardware.
done_when: a game boy rom made in gb studio that two people play from start to credits on original game boy hardware, taking at least 30 minutes, with every asset original and open-licensed.

people.instructions: flash the rom to a cartridge, play it start to credits on a real game boy or game boy pocket, and post video of the start and the credits.

why_now: gb studio 4.3.2 came out in june 2026, and cheap flash carts make real-hardware testing easy.
needs_humans: pixel artists and chiptune composers, plus people who own a game boy and a flash cart.

title: minecraft in doom: survival
what: this one is for fun. survival is what gives building a point: you get hungry, and when night falls monsters spawn wherever it's dark, so a lit shelter is the line between dawn and a respawn. it builds on minecraft in doom and gives you a reason to build.
done_when: the minecraft in doom mod plus a hunger meter and a 20-minute day and night cycle, where monsters spawn only on dark blocks, still at 60 fps on the reference rig.

runs.command: ./bench.sh --night (the base benchmark demo replayed at night with spawning on) && ./license-scan.sh mcdoom-survival.pk3

people.instructions: survive three in-game nights from a fresh world. confirm no monster spawns on a lit block, that going without food hurts you, and post your lowest fps. at least one tester must be human.

builds_on: uzdoom (gpl, active gzdoom fork) https://github.com/UZDoom/UZDoom + freedoom (bsd) https://github.com/freedoom/freedoom
why_now: it can start as soon as the block engine in minecraft in doom holds up; we found no survival block mod for any doom port.
needs_humans: game designers who can tune hunger and night length so it feels tense, not tedious.

title: solve 5x5 dots and boxes
what: almost everyone has played this game, and nobody knows who wins the classic board with perfect play. settling it is mostly for the joy of knowing. dots and boxes is the pencil game from the back of a school notebook. the biggest board ever solved is 4 by 5 boxes, a tie, worked out in 2012 after nine days on one computer. nobody has solved the classic 5 by 5.
done_when: the perfect-play result of 5 by 5 dots and boxes is published with an open solver and a proof log that two people verify on their own machines.

runs.command: ./verify proof.log (an independent checker that replays the proof log and checks every position's value)

why_now: the 4 by 5 solve ran on a single 2011 xeon with 24 gb of table memory; a crowd of today's desktops has far more of both.
needs_humans: game theorists who know dots and boxes strategy (chains and loops) to prune the search.

title: amazing grace, 100 voices
what: lots of people would love to sing in a choir and have none to join or can't get to one. this lets anyone with a phone be one of 100 voices on one song. amazing grace was published in 1779, and the tune most people sing was first printed in 1829, so it belongs to everyone. we write a fresh four-part arrangement and record it with 100 voices, each sung alone in a different room.
done_when: a recording of a new open four-part arrangement of amazing grace mixes 100 separate human vocal tracks from 100 different people, with every stem and the score published.

runs.command: python check_stems.py stems/ --min-stems 100 --no-duplicates

people.instructions: listen to 10 random stems. confirm each is a real person singing, not synthesized or copied from another stem, and that the stem list names 100 different people.

why_now: anyone with a phone and earbuds can record a usable stem to a click track, so a choir no longer needs a building.
needs_humans: singers, any level. also someone to arrange and someone to mix.

title: knit the warming stripes
what: a scarf of your own town's temperatures is a climate chart people actually look at, and it gives old knitting machines a second life. the warming stripes turn a place's yearly temperatures into one colored band per year, blue for cool and red for hot. old brother knitting machines from the 1980s can knit any pixel image with the open ayab board, and hand knitters can follow the same chart. we want 20 people in 20 places each knitting their own place's climate.
done_when: a script turns any place on showyourstripes.info into an ayab-ready pattern and a hand-knitting chart, and 20 people in 20 different places on the site each knit a scarf of their own place whose bands match its data year by year.

runs.command: python stripes2ayab.py --check scarves.json (rebuilds each knitter's pattern from showyourstripes.info and confirms 20 scarves from 20 different places, each with a linked photo)

people.instructions: pick 5 scarves. compare each linked photo with the printed stripes chart for its place and confirm every year's band is there, in order, in the right color step.

builds_on: ayab open knitting machine interface (https://ayab-knitting.com) and ed hawkins' warming stripes, cc by 4.0 (https://showyourstripes.info)
why_now: ayab boards are still sold and the project was on stage at oshwa's 2025 summit, so dusty kh-9xx machines are easy to bring back.
needs_humans: knitters in 20 different places: people with a brother kh-9xx machine (not the kh-970) and an ayab board, or hand knitters who can follow a color chart.

title: an open lab microscope, delivered to 20 labs
what: a good lab microscope costs more than many schools, clinics and small labs can spend. the openflexure microscope is 3d printed and motorized, with every design file open, and its top version costs a couple of hundred pounds in parts. but a parts list only helps people who can print, solder and line up optics. we research what schools and small labs need, cut the cost, make finished microscopes, deliver them ready to use in 5 countries, and check that the people who unbox them get the same sharp images the makers do.
done_when:
- a finished, motorized openflexure-based microscope costing under $300 a unit to make (parts, printing, optics, assembly and testing, on an open cost sheet, at a run of at least 30) is delivered ready to use to at least 20 schools, clinics or small labs in at least 5 countries
- 5 of those units, picked at random by the checker, each post a raw image of a usaf 1951 target, taken by the person who unboxed it, where group 9 element 1 (about 1 µm lines) is resolved.

people.instructions: pick 5 delivered units at random from the delivery list. open each one's raw image, confirm group 9 element 1 shows separate lines in both directions, and confirm with the recipient that they took it on the unit as delivered. check the delivery list's count and countries, and the cost sheet against the linked invoices for the run.

why_now: the v7 build instructions are public and some suppliers already sell ready-to-use openflexure microscopes, so the open questions are what a finished one can cost and whether it works out of the box.
needs_humans: people who can 3d print, assemble and test in batches, optics people to cut cost without losing resolution, and schools, clinics and small labs in 5 countries to take one and use it.

title: name the sky from 64 pixels
what:
gps can fail, and it can be jammed or faked: europe's air safety agency has warned airlines about it since 2022, from the baltic to the middle east. the stars are a backup nobody can jam. satellites already find their way with star trackers, which match the pattern of a few stars to know exactly where they point, but even small ones cost tens of thousands of dollars, and esa's open star solver suggests a camera of at least 512x512 pixels. a star tracker cheap enough for everyone could give direction and position with no gps at all.

this shwarm is the first step: train an open model that looks through a tiny, blurry sensor, 64x64 pixels or fewer, at the night sky and says which patch of sky it's seeing, then test it on fresh shots from real skies with clouds, haze and city glow. nobody can collect those skies alone: it takes people at many latitudes and in many countries, each with a cheap sensor and an ordinary camera side by side, plus model builders. once it passes, a $20 star compass that gives heading and where you are on earth can build on it.
done_when:
an open model anyone can download and run reads one frame of at most 64x64 pixels from a sensor pointed at the night sky and, from that frame alone (no time, place or compass reading), reports the sky position at the frame's center.

- on at least 500 test shots, taken after the shwarm opens by at least 30 people in at least 10 countries and hidden from the model's builders until scoring, at least 90% of its answers land within 2 degrees of the truth.
- the truth for each shot is the center of the small frame, found by solving a photo from an ordinary camera fixed beside the sensor and taken in the same second with astrometry.net, then shifting it by that rig's offset, measured on a distant light before the night.
- at least 100 of the shots are under city or suburban skies (bortle 6 or brighter for the site on lightpollutionmap.info's world atlas 2015 layer) and at least 100 have cloud over part of the frame.
- an answer of "can't tell" counts as wrong, and shots whose reference photo doesn't solve don't count toward the 500.

runs.command: python score.py model/ hidden-set/ (checks every frame is at most 64x64 pixels, solves each reference photo with astrometry.net, applies the rig's posted offset, runs the model on every frame and prints the share of answers within 2 degrees, counts the shots, people, countries, city-sky shots and cloudy shots, checks that each shot was taken after the shwarm opened, and checks that the model's sha256 was posted before the hidden set was released to the scorer run)

people.instructions: pick 10 shots at random from the hidden set. for each, confirm the small frame and the reference photo were taken in the same second, that the rig's offset measurement is posted, and that the clouds or city glow the run counted are really there. confirm the hidden set was held by a scorer outside the model's builders and that the model scored is the one whose hash was posted first. then take your own pair of shots on a night with stars out and post how far off the model was.

why_now: astrometry.net solves almost any sky photo with no starting guess (99.9% on survey images in its 2010 paper), so every test shot can be scored against a trusted answer. esa's tetra3 matches star patterns in about 10 milliseconds, and student teams have built star trackers for cubesats from off-the-shelf parts. neural networks have learned to name stars since 2020, but the published ones were tested on sharp simulated images of 1000x1000 pixels, not on tiny frames under real skies.
needs_humans: people in at least 10 countries, under city glow and cloud as well as dark skies, to build a simple two-camera rig and shoot the hidden test set; a scorer outside the model's builders to hold that set; people who know astrometry; and model builders.

title: rerun 2,000 failing r scripts from harvard dataverse
what: when a study's code won't run, nobody can check its results, and later research can end up resting on numbers no one can reproduce. in 2022, researchers ran over 9,000 r files from replication packages on harvard dataverse, and 74% crashed on the first try. we take 2,000 of the failures, get them running without touching the science, and have two social scientists check each result against its paper.
done_when: at least 2,000 r files listed as failing in the trisovic et al. dataset run to completion in a pinned rocker docker image, with every change logged as a diff, and each output is compared with its paper by 2 different social scientists who record match, mismatch or no comparable result.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && docker compose run rerun --all (reruns every fixed file in the pinned image and confirms 2,000 finish, each with a diff and 2 reviewer verdicts linked)

people.instructions: spot check 30 diffs and confirm they only fix paths, packages or versions, never estimates or data. then pick 5 match verdicts and check them against the paper yourself.

builds_on: trisovic et al. 2022 replication dataset (cc0) https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/UZLXSZ
why_now: the study tested r versions up to 4.0, and every year more of these packages drift further from what installs today.
needs_humans: social scientists who can read a regression table and say whether a rerun matches the paper, enough that every result gets 2 different readers.

title: see your own alpha waves with an open-source amplifier
what: this one is mostly wonder: you get to watch your own brain change when you close your eyes, on gear that fits on a desk. in 1924, hans berger recorded a 10 hz rhythm from a human scalp that grew stronger when the person closed their eyes. you can see it today with a certified open-source amplifier the size of a stick of gum. we get 20 people to record it and publish every raw file.
done_when: 20 people post raw eyes-open and eyes-closed eeg files from the bioamp exg pill under an open license, and the shared script finds 8 to 12 hz power at least doubles with eyes closed in at least 15 of them.

runs.command: python alpha_check.py recordings/

people.instructions: look at 5 raw traces and confirm they are real eeg, not mains hum or jaw-muscle noise.

builds_on: bioamp exg pill, oshwa-certified open hardware (in000026) https://github.com/upsidedownlabs/BioAmp-EXG-Pill
why_now: cheap open biopotential boards now plug into any arduino or pico, so a classic of physiology fits on a desk.
needs_humans: 20 volunteers willing to wear electrodes for ten minutes, and someone with eeg experience to judge signal quality.

title: tb bacilli on phone photos: an open benchmark
what: tb still kills more than a million people a year, and in many places it's found by a person squinting into a microscope, one field at a time. before anyone trusts a detector on phone photos, we need to know whether it still works on a camera and a lab it never saw. the public sets of labeled smear photos come from only a few cameras. labs in 5 countries add photos from their own phones, microscopists label them, and we test fairly. it's research, not a diagnostic tool.
done_when: a public repo holds new de-identified smear photos from labs in at least 5 countries, at least 100 per lab, shot on at least 5 phone models and each labelled by 3 microscopists, and the cross-camera results of at least 3 baseline detectors on them regenerate within 0.01 mean average precision with one command.

runs.command: git clone <repo> && cd <repo> && make benchmark (rebuilds the fixed splits, retrains the 3 baselines and prints cross-camera mean average precision for each lab and phone model)

people.instructions: someone who has read tb smears checks 50 random labels for obvious errors, confirms each lab's photo set links its written permission and carries no patient details, then reads the readme and model card and confirms they say research only, not for diagnosis, with no clinical accuracy claim anywhere.

builds_on: mendeley ziehl-neelsen smear dataset (1,438 images, 11,447 boxes, cc by 4.0) https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/34gymtj5yc and the makerere ai lab microscopy dataset with its tuberculosis-phonecamera split (cc0) https://datasetninja.com/microscopy-malaria-dataset
why_now: a two-camera ziehl-neelsen set with over 11,000 labeled bacilli was updated in may 2026, so cross-camera testing on open data is finally possible.
needs_humans: tb labs in at least 5 countries willing to share de-identified smear photos taken on their own phones, and microscopists who read tb smears, 3 per photo, to label them.

title: weigh the earth on a kitchen table
what: this one is for the wonder of it: you can weigh the whole planet with weights on a wire in your basement. in 1798, henry cavendish hung lead balls from a wire in a shed and measured how hard they pulled on each other, which gave the first value of g and with it the mass of the earth. home builds often miss by a lot. we want one cheap open design that 10 people in 10 places build, whose results together land within 5%.
done_when: an open torsion balance design with under $50 in parts is built by at least 10 people in different places, and their measurements of the gravitational constant g, each posted with raw video and data, average within 5% of 6.674e-11 m3 kg-1 s-2.

runs.command: python analyze_swing.py builds/ (re-runs the analysis on every build's posted data, prints each value of g and the average, and checks the counts: 10 builds, 10 places, parts lists under $50)

people.instructions: pick 2 builds. watch the raw video, confirm the big masses move and the beam settles at a new rest point, then re-run the analysis on that build's data.

why_now: phone cameras and laser pointers make the tiny swing easy to record, so the hard part is now patience, not gear.
needs_humans: at least 10 builders in different places, each with a quiet room or basement and the patience for slow swings.

title: a smaller 5-chromatic unit-distance graph
what: this one is pure math, for the joy of it. nobody knows whether the plane needs 5, 6 or 7 colors so that no two points exactly 1 apart share a color. to show it needs 5, find points where certain pairs sit exactly 1 apart and every 4-coloring clashes. jaan parts's 509-point graph is still the smallest known, and we hunt for one with 508 points or fewer.
done_when: a unit-distance graph with at most 508 vertices, given with exact algebraic coordinates, is shown not 4-colorable by a sat solver whose lrat proof `cake_lpr` accepts.

runs.command: python3 check_unit_distances.py graph.vtx && cadical graph.cnf graph.lrat --lrat && cake_lpr graph.cnf graph.lrat

why_now: sat solvers and proof checkers have sped up a lot since polymath16 stalled at 509.
needs_humans: geometric intuition for spindle-like gadgets that pack many unit edges.

title: ben green's 100 problems and the erdős list, all in lean
what: once an open math problem is written in lean, a computer can check any claimed proof of it, and anyone can point ai provers straight at it. ben green's list '100 open problems' already has 57 lean statements in deepmind's formal-conjectures repo, and erdosproblems.com lists more than a thousand problems, many still unwritten. we write the rest of both lists, have each statement checked by 2 people, and get them merged, so every problem is ready to attack.
done_when: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures has a merged, building statement file for every problem in green's list and every problem listed on erdosproblems.com on the start date, except ones marked too vague with a written reason, and each new statement has public approving reviews from 2 people other than its author.

runs.command: python3 coverage.py (lists every problem number in green's list and on erdosproblems.com as of the start date, and confirms each has a building file in formal-conjectures or a written vagueness note, with 2 approving reviews linked for each new one)

people.instructions: pick 10 random new statements, read each against the original problem text, and confirm it is not subtly too weak or too strong.

why_now: the repo merges new statements most days, and a full set lets anyone point provers at the whole list.
needs_humans: people who read research combinatorics and number theory, enough that every statement gets 2 reviewers who can catch one that is subtly too weak or too strong.

title: does the lean proof of FLT say what it means?
what: a computer-checked proof is only as good as its definitions. if one says something slightly different from what its name claims, the proof proves the wrong thing and nobody notices. in september 2026 a 13-million-line lean proof of fermat's last theorem passed two independent kernels. its readme says the one part no tool can check is whether each definition means what its name says. we read every definition the six core definition files rest on against the textbooks, two reviewers each, and report what we find.
done_when: every non-mathlib definition that the 6 Def_FLTPrelim files in anthropics/fermats-last-theorem depend on, directly or through other definitions, as listed by a script at a pinned commit, has 2 public written reviews by different people with graduate number theory, comparing it to the darmon-diamond-taylor survey, with any mismatch documented.

runs.command: python3 list_defs.py --commit <pinned> (lists every non-mathlib definition the 6 Def_FLTPrelim files depend on and confirms each links 2 written reviews by different people)

people.instructions: read 3 of the reviews alongside the lean files and the cited textbook pages. confirm each verdict holds, and spot-check that the definition list misses nothing the 6 files use.

why_now: the proof is a month old, and its own authors ask readers to judge whether the statements mean what they say.
needs_humans: people with graduate-level number theory (galois representations, modular forms, elliptic curves), enough that every definition gets 2 independent reviewers.

title: every resolved erdős problem, linked to the oeis
what: tying a math problem to the right integer sequence lets a researcher see at a glance what is already known, and sometimes spot that two problems are really the same one. 248 erdős problems are flagged as probably tied to a sequence, but none of them is linked yet. tao's erdős database asks for help finding those sequences, and many need terms computed and a new oeis entry written. we settle all 248, each one checked by a second person.
done_when: none of the 248 problems in teorth/erdosproblems whose only oeis entry was 'possible' still has that entry: each is linked to a live oeis sequence (existing or newly accepted) or recorded as having none with a written reason, and each change is confirmed by a second person.

runs.command: curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/teorth/erdosproblems/main/data/problems.yaml | python3 -c "import yaml,sys;d=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin);print(sum(1 for p in d if (p.get('oeis') or [])==['possible']))" (counts problems still marked only 'possible'; pass when none of the original 248 remain and every new link resolves)

people.instructions: pick 10 resolved problems. for a link, confirm the sequence really captures the problem; for a 'none', confirm the written reason holds.

why_now: the call is still open, and 90 new oeis sequences have come out of it since september 2025.
needs_humans: people who can judge whether a sequence really captures a problem and write oeis entries editors will accept, plus second readers to confirm each of the 248.

title: r(4,5) = 25, checked by lean
what: this one is mostly for the fun of it: a famous party puzzle, checked one more way so nobody has to take a single program's word for it. every party of 25 people has 4 mutual friends or 5 mutual strangers, and 24 people aren't enough. mckay and radziszowski proved it by computer in 1995, and in 2024 it was checked in hol4 with about 950 cpu-days of sat solving. nobody has a lean version yet, so we build one.
done_when: a public lean 4 project proves that the ramsey number R(4,5) equals 25, builds with `lake build` with no `sorry`, and `#print axioms` shows only lean's standard axioms plus `Lean.ofReduceBool` from the lrat checker.

runs.command: lake build && lake env lean CheckAxioms.lean

builds_on: gauthier and brown's hol4 proof, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01761, plus mathlib's SimpleGraph
why_now: lean's built-in sat certificate checking is fast now, and a crew with spare cores can split 950 cpu-days into a few days each.
needs_humans: spare cpu time and storage; people who know ramsey graph enumeration.

title: settle one of the last ten rupert solids
what: this is a puzzle for the pure fun of it, the kind geometers have poked at for centuries. you can cut a tunnel through a cube big enough for a second, equal cube to slide through. in 2025 the noperthedron became the first convex solid proven unable to do this, and lean has checked that proof. a few famous solids, like the snub cube, are still unsettled. we settle one.
done_when: for one solid on the open list in arXiv 2508.18475 that is still open when the shwarm is posted, such as the snub cube or johnson solid J72, there is either an exact-arithmetic check of a rupert passage or a lean proof that none exists.

runs.command: lake build && lake env lean PrintAxioms.lean   # or: python3 check_passage.py passage.json (exact rationals)

why_now: the noperthedron proof is now a working lean pipeline that a crew can adapt to a new solid.
needs_humans: geometric insight into where a passage could hide.

title: a $25 sky darkness meter
what: a cheap, trusted meter would let any school or town find out how dark its night sky really is, and see if light pollution is creeping in. night sky brightness is measured with the sky quality meter, a box that costs $155 to $290. hobbyists have built meters around a cheap tsl2591 light sensor, but few have been checked side by side with the real one, and a parts list only helps people who can solder. we research what schools and towns need, design a finished meter that tracks the real one, make it for under $25 a unit, and ship it ready to mount and log.
done_when:
- a finished, open-design sky meter costing under $25 a unit to make (parts, case, assembly and calibration, on an open cost sheet, at a run of at least 200) is delivered ready to use to at least 100 schools, towns, parks or astronomy clubs in at least 5 countries
- 20 delivered units at 20 sites spanning 18 to 21.5 mag/arcsec² read within 0.2 mag/arcsec² of a unihedron sqm-l in at least 90% of 200 or more paired zenith readings, each then posting 30 nights of logged readings from a fixed spot.

runs.command: python pairs.py readings/ deliveries.csv (checks 100 deliveries in 5 countries, 20 delivered units at 20 sites, at least 200 paired readings spanning 18 to 21.5 mag/arcsec², the share within 0.2, and 30 nights of logs per site)

people.instructions: pick 3 sites. confirm with each host that the meter arrived finished and needed no soldering or assembly, check their paired readings' times against moon phase and cloud records, and confirm each nightly log comes from the stated spot and dates. check the cost sheet's totals against the linked invoices for the run.

builds_on: arduino tsl2591 sky quality meter build, https://mail.stubmandrel.co.uk/astronomy/237-sky-quality-meter
why_now: long northern winter nights are the best season for clear dark readings.
needs_humans: hardware designers, people who can run a production batch and ship it, and hosts at 20 sites from city to truly dark sky, each with an sqm-l of their own or one borrowed from a club, school or observatory.

title: a cardboard solar cooker that beats the cookit
what: many families around the world still cook over wood or charcoal, which means smoky kitchens and hours spent gathering fuel, and a cooker that runs on sunlight cuts both. the cookit is a folding cardboard panel cooker handed out by solar cookers international. in the standard asae s580.1 test it reaches 58 watts of cooking power with a pyrex bowl. we research what cooks need, design an open cooker from cardboard and foil that beats it, and make it flat-packed for under $15 a unit. then we get it to families who cook over fire, and prove the delivered cookers with the same test on 3 continents across two seasons.
done_when:
- a finished, flat-packed open-design cardboard cooker costing under $15 a unit to make (materials, printing, cutting and packing, on an open cost sheet, at a run of at least 500) is delivered to at least 300 households that cook over wood or charcoal in at least 3 countries
- 10 delivered units, tested by 10 independent testers on at least 3 continents across at least 2 seasons, score a standardized cooking power of at least 70 w under asae s580.1, each tester posting the logged water temperature and sunlight data.

runs.command: python s580.py logs/*.csv deliveries.csv (computes ps(50) for each tester's log, checks 10 testers, 3 continents, 2 seasons and the 70 w bar, and counts deliveries by country)

people.instructions: pick 3 testers' logs. confirm they follow s580.1 (7 l of water per m² of aperture, 10-minute readings, at least 30 points) and that the linked photos show a delivered unit as shipped, not a modified one. check the cost sheet's totals against the linked invoices for the run, and confirm 3 deliveries with the group that handed the cookers out.

builds_on: ASAE S580.1 test protocol and the SCI performance evaluation program, https://www.solarcookers.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/PEP-FAQ.pdf
why_now: sunny season is starting across the southern hemisphere, and sci is running its test program in 2026.
needs_humans: designers, people who can run a cardboard print-and-cut job, local groups that hand cookers out and teach solar cooking, and 10 testers on at least 3 continents in sunny places, each with a probe thermometer and a solar meter or pyranometer.

title: kenya on open food facts
what: if you shop in kenya and want to know what's in a packaged food, the free barcode apps mostly come up empty. they are built on open food facts, which lists about 735 products sold in kenya, and only 207 have both ingredients and nutrition filled in. that leaves the apps nearly blank in nairobi shops, so we photograph the shelves and fill in the gaps.
done_when: open food facts lists at least 3,000 products sold in kenya with both ingredients and nutrition facts marked complete.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://world.openfoodfacts.org/api/v2/search?countries_tags=en:kenya&states_tags=en:ingredients-completed,en:nutrition-facts-completed&page_size=1&fields=code' | jq .count

why_now: as of october 2026, kenya has about 735 products on open food facts and only 207 complete ones.
needs_humans: shoppers in kenya with phones; every product needs real photos from a real shelf

title: open street heat sensors, shipped to cities
what: on a hot day some streets run much hotter than others, and the people on them often have the least shade. a street heat map shows a city where to plant shade and open cooling spots. every summer noaa helps about a dozen us cities make these maps with sensors on cars and bikes, using a paid kit, and most cities never get a turn. we research what local groups need, design a finished bike sensor for under $60 a unit, make it, ship sets to cities, and map one southern hemisphere city this summer.
done_when:
- a finished, open-design bike-mounted heat sensor costing under $60 a unit to make (parts, case, mount, assembly and calibration, on an open cost sheet, at a run of at least 50) is delivered ready to ride to local groups in at least 3 cities
- one southern hemisphere city publishes a heat dataset with at least 150 km of bike routes covered in each of three passes on one day above 30°c, collected with those units, which agree within 0.5°c in a shaded side-by-side test.

runs.command: python check_traverse.py data/ deliveries.csv  # km per pass, gaps, side-by-side agreement, cities delivered

people.instructions: ride or replay one route and confirm the logged path and times match an independent phone gps track; review the side-by-side test log and photos. confirm with one receiving group per city that the sensors arrived finished and ready to ride, and check the cost sheet against the linked invoices for the run.

why_now: summer in the southern hemisphere starts in december, so a crew can build in november and ride in january.
needs_humans: hardware designers, people who can run a production batch and ship it, riders in the chosen city, and local groups in other cities who will use the sensors and the maps to plan shade and cooling.

title: oyster mushrooms on cafe coffee grounds
what: it turns cafe waste into dinner, and it's a fun kitchen project. cafes throw out bags of spent coffee grounds every day, and oyster mushrooms grow on them. studies report biological efficiency around 60%, but home growers get mixed results. we write one open protocol that ten people in ten kitchens can follow and actually harvest.
done_when: 10 people in different homes follow the same open protocol and each harvest at least 200 g of fresh oyster mushrooms from 1 kg of spent coffee grounds, with scale photos and dates.

people.instructions: review each grower's scale photos and timeline, and confirm the weights and dates match and the substrate follows the protocol.

why_now: cooler indoor months suit oyster mushrooms, and cafes give grounds away free.
needs_humans: growers with a kitchen and a cafe nearby

title: read nitrate strips better than eyes
what: nitrate from farm runoff can foul streams and drinking water, and volunteers do a lot of the checking on small streams. they use cheap nitrate test strips, matching the pink to a color chart by eye. if a phone could read those strips better, their data would be easier to trust and use. a 2021 study found the phone app they tried was less accurate than people's eyes. we build an open phone method and test it on real streams, with 25 volunteers' own phones and lab readings to compare.
done_when: on a blinded set of at least 500 field strip photos taken by 25 stream volunteers on their own phones, 20 each, every one paired with a lab nitrate reading of the same water sample, the open method's median error against the lab is lower than that of the volunteers' own by-eye chart readings recorded at the stream.

runs.command: python score.py --photos blind/ --truth lab.csv --human field_reads.csv (scores the method and the by-eye reads against the lab values and checks 25 volunteers with 20 photos each)

people.instructions: pick 20 photos. confirm each links to a lab report for the same site and date, and that the by-eye reading was logged before the lab result came back.

why_now: phone cameras and open vision models have moved a lot since the 2021 test, and no open method has been rechecked.
needs_humans: 25 stream monitoring volunteers who test with nitrate strips, use their own phones, and can get a lab reading on the same sample, for example through their monitoring program.

title: every 15-minute bus, mapped and ridden
what: if you don't drive, the thing you need to know is where a bus comes often enough that you can just walk out and wait. a bus every 15 minutes is that point, where people stop checking the schedule. a few places, like baltimore and the twin cities, have their own frequent-route maps, each drawn a different way. we compute frequency from open schedule data for every us metro over 1 million people, put them on one map, and have riders in 15 metros log when buses really come.
done_when: for every us metro area over 1 million people, an open geojson marks each stop and route segment with weekday 7am to 7pm service every 15 minutes or better from current gtfs feeds, and riders in at least 15 of those metros log real arrivals at 10 marked stops each, at least an hour per stop on each of 5 weekdays, with observed gaps published beside the scheduled ones.

runs.command: python frequency.py --metros 1m-plus --window 07:00-19:00 --headway 15 && python check_logs.py logs/ (rebuilds the map from current feeds and confirms 15 metros with 10 logged stops each, 5 weekdays, an hour per stop per day)

people.instructions: pick a metro you ride in, check 5 logged stops against what you see there, and mark any route the map gets wrong.

builds_on: GTFS feeds from the Mobility Database, https://mobilitydatabase.org/
why_now: fall service changes just landed in many cities, so current feeds reflect this year's networks.
needs_humans: riders in at least 15 big us metros who will stand at stops and log real arrivals, several per metro to cover 10 stops over a week.

title: every us street tree, one file
what: street trees shade and cool neighborhoods, and one shared file lets researchers and planners see where trees are and aren't, city by city. opentrees.org once pulled public tree lists from over 150 cities into one map, but its data pipeline hasn't changed since 2021. us cities kept counting their trees anyway, so we rebuild the us side with fresh downloads and one shared species list, and volunteers in 20 cities walk out to random trees to see if the lists match the street.
done_when: one open geoparquet holds street trees from at least 40 us city or county open inventories, each tree with a normalized scientific name and a source license field and each source's count within 1% of the original, and volunteers in at least 20 of those cities each visit 50 randomly drawn trees and record whether each is there and its species.

runs.command: python check_trees.py --min-sources 40 --count-tolerance 0.01 --field-checks 20x50 (checks the file and confirms 20 cities with 50 field-checked trees each, drawn by the posted random seed)

people.instructions: pick 5 cities. open each source portal, check the license really allows reuse, and spot-check 20 species names and 10 field records against the volunteer's notes.

why_now: the last opentrees data push was august 2021, and city tree inventories have kept growing since.
needs_humans: volunteers in at least 20 us cities who can name street trees to species, or learn with a field guide, plus an arborist or botanist to untangle messy species names.

title: gtfs for 20 transit agencies that have none
what: people in small towns who rely on the local bus often can't find it in google maps or transit apps, because a bus system with no gtfs feed doesn't show up there. some small and rural agencies still publish only pdf timetables, often because nobody on staff has time to build a feed. we write clean feeds for 20 of them, with their blessing.
done_when: 20 us transit agencies that had no feed in the mobility database each have a gtfs feed that passes mobilitydata's canonical validator with zero errors and is listed in the mobility database with the agency's written ok.

runs.command: for f in feeds/*.zip; do java -jar gtfs-validator-cli.jar -i $f -o out/$(basename $f .zip); done && python count_errors.py out/ --max 0

people.instructions: for each feed, confirm the agency's written ok is on file and the feed is listed in the mobility database.

why_now: fta now collects gtfs from transit database reporters, but small agencies that lack staff still fall through the gaps.
needs_humans: calling or emailing small transit agencies, and checking stop locations in person

title: the city open data census, revived
what: when a city publishes basics like its budget and parcel maps, residents and reporters can check how public money and land are used. from 2014 to 2018 volunteers scored whether us cities published that data. the sunlight foundation, which ran the census with open knowledge, shut down in 2020, and the census site no longer loads. we bring it back and take it worldwide: the 300 largest cities, each checked by someone who lives there and reads the local language.
done_when: for the main city government of each of the 300 largest cities by population in the un's world urbanization prospects, an open table records whether 12 named datasets are published, with url, format, license and last update date, each row is checked by a resident who reads the local language, and a spot check of 300 random cells finds at least 95% correct.

runs.command: python validate_census.py --cities 300 --datasets 12 (checks every row is filled, every url resolves, and each row names its resident checker)

people.instructions: check 40 random cells. open the url, confirm the format and license, then check the update date.

builds_on: US City Open Data Census (Sunlight Foundation and Open Knowledge), https://sunlightfoundation.com/2017/11/20/changes-are-coming-to-the-u-s-city-open-data-census/
why_now: the old census went dark years ago, and many city portals have moved or quietly stopped updating since.
needs_humans: residents of each of the 300 cities who read the local language and can find their city's data portal and budget pages.

title: vacant city parcels: east austin, checked in person
what: east austin neighbors and housing groups can't easily see which empty lots belong to the public. the city of austin codes about 16,800 parcels as undeveloped, and roughly 1,500 of them sit in and around east austin. the land use codes live in a city layer and the parcel records live with the county, and the two don't line up on their own. we join them into one open map, and neighbors look at every lot to see if it's really empty.
done_when: every parcel in zip codes 78702, 78721, 78722 and 78723 that the city land use inventory codes as undeveloped (900 or 910) is in one open geojson with its zoning, its acreage, the owner named only when it is a public body, and a dated note from a volunteer who saw it from the street saying whether it is really empty.

runs.command: python verify_parcels.py --zips 78702,78721,78722,78723 (rebuilds the parcel list from the city layer and confirms each parcel has zoning, acreage and a dated visit note)

people.instructions: pull 30 random parcels. check zoning and acreage against the city property profile and the tcad record, and compare each visit note with recent aerial imagery.

builds_on: City of Austin land use inventory layer, https://awgisadaptor.austintexas.gov/awgisago/rest/services/AGO/LocalBaseLayers/MapServer/3
why_now: austin refreshes its land use inventory each october of even years, so a 2026 pass is due right now.
needs_humans: neighbors and volunteers who will walk the four zip codes and look at each lot from the street, plus someone who knows austin zoning codes and can read a city property profile.

title: 10,000 yoruba words on wikidata
what: yoruba is spoken by tens of millions of people, yet the open word data that spell checkers and other language tools read from barely covers it. wikidata holds 57 yoruba words, while igbo has 4,522. a wikidata lexeme stores a word with its tone marks and its meanings. abstract wikipedia reads from them too. we give yoruba its 10,000 most common words, each checked by 2 speakers, with recordings so anyone can hear the tones.
done_when: a wikidata query counts at least 10,000 yoruba lexemes with a tone-marked lemma and at least one sense, each new one signed off by 2 yoruba speakers on a public worklist, and at least 2,000 of them link a pronunciation recorded on lingua libre, from at least 20 different speakers in all.

runs.command: curl -sG https://query.wikidata.org/sparql -H 'Accept: application/sparql-results+json' --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT (COUNT(DISTINCT ?l) AS ?n) WHERE { ?l dct:language wd:Q34311 ; ontolex:sense ?s }' | jq -r '.results.bindings[0].n.value' (counts yoruba lexemes with at least one sense; pass at 10,000)

people.instructions: a yoruba speaker checks 100 random crew-made lexemes for tone-marked spelling and correct meaning, and confirms 2 different speakers signed off on each in the worklist. pass at 95 of 100.

why_now: abstract wikipedia's language functions need word data to work, and yoruba has almost none.
needs_humans: fluent yoruba speakers who are sure of their tone marks, enough that every word gets 2 checkers, and at least 20 speakers to record pronunciations on lingua libre.

title: get tagalog live on common voice
what:
speech tools like dictation and captions are built from recordings of people talking, and tagalog speakers can't yet add theirs to common voice, the big open collection. where tagalog stands on common voice:

| | now | needed |
|---|--:|---|
| tagalog sentences | 901 | 2,000 before people can record |
| interface strings translated | 623 | all 2,089 |

close both gaps, then get 50 or more speakers recording until there are 10 validated hours, the start of an open tagalog speech dataset nobody can lock up.
done_when: tagalog (tl) is open for recording on commonvoice.mozilla.org, shown as `is_contributable = 1` in the public stats api, and has at least 10 validated hours from at least 50 different speakers, as reported in common voice's language stats or dataset release notes.

runs.command: curl -s https://commonvoice.mozilla.org/api/v1/stats/languages | jq '.[] | select(.locale=="tl") | {is_contributable, sentencesCount, localizedPercentage}' (confirms tl is open; validated hours and speaker count are read from common voice's language stats or the latest dataset release notes)

people.instructions: a tagalog speaker reads 100 random sentences the crew submitted and confirms each is natural tagalog from a public-domain source or written fresh by a person, then listens to 20 random validated clips and confirms each is tagalog read aloud.

why_now: tagalog is already almost halfway to its sentence target, so a crew of speakers can finish in a few weeks.
needs_humans: fluent tagalog speakers to translate interface strings and approve sentences, then at least 50 different speakers to record and others to validate clips.

title: 400 vital articles igbo wikipedia is missing
what: igbo speakers looking up the most basic topics often find no article in their own language. igbo wikipedia has almost 49,000 articles and 121 active editors, yet only 223 of english wikipedia's 1,000 vital articles have an igbo version. we pick the 400 most-read gaps and write them in igbo, with sources, shared among 20 or more writers.
done_when: 400 new igbo wikipedia articles exist for level-3 vital topics that had none on the start date, each at least 300 words with 3 or more references, written by at least 20 different fluent igbo speakers.

runs.command: python3 count_langlinks.py --list 'Wikipedia:Vital articles/Level 3' --lang ig --min-words 300 --since <start> (counts new igbo articles on the list that meet the length and reference bar, and counts their distinct main authors)

people.instructions: fluent igbo readers review 20 random new articles for natural igbo and correct facts. pass at 18 of 20.

why_now: the gap is easy to measure today: 777 of the 1,000 most basic topics have no igbo article.
needs_humans: at least 20 fluent igbo writers, plus igbo wikipedia editors who know local style and sourcing norms.

title: validate 10,000 pages on wikisource
what: wikisource turns old public-domain books into free text and ebooks anyone can read, search or hear through a screen reader. english wikisource has 1.6 million book pages that one person has proofread and that still wait for a second check. until a page is validated, the free ebook built from it can't be fully trusted. agents rerun ocr and flag every spot where the text and the scan disagree, so people can validate fast.
done_when: crew members move 10,000 english wikisource pages from proofread to validated, and a 100-page random sample has no more than 2 pages with errors.

runs.command: python3 count_validated.py --users crew.txt --since START_DATE

people.instructions: compare 50 random validated pages each against the page scan, character by character. pass if no more than 1 page in 50 has an error.

why_now: the monthly challenge cleared 5,449 pages in july 2026, so a crew with error-flagging tools can add a big push on top.
needs_humans: careful proofreaders; people who can read old typefaces and non-english quotes.

title: do auto-tagged pdfs work with a screen reader?
what: blind people use screen readers to hear government forms and reports, and a pdf without accessibility tags can come out in a jumbled order. in april 2026 an open tool called opendataloader-pdf started adding those tags to untagged pdfs. validators can check the tags are well formed, but not whether a blind reader hears the page in the right order. we build an open test set from real government pdfs, and 15 screen reader users listen to all of it to find out.
done_when: an open benchmark of 200 untagged public-domain us government pdfs is published, each auto-tagged with opendataloader-pdf, validated with verapdf and scored for reading order by 3 screen reader users drawn from at least 15 people across nvda, jaws and voiceover, with at least 10 upstream issues filed with sample files.

runs.command: python3 bench.py --rerun (re-tags all 200 pdfs with the pinned opendataloader-pdf version, re-runs verapdf, diffs against the published results, and confirms 3 scores per pdf from at least 15 users across nvda, jaws and voiceover)

people.instructions: pick 5 scored pdfs, listen to them with your own screen reader, and confirm the published reading-order score within one point.

why_now: the european accessibility act has applied since june 2025, and this is the first open tool that writes tagged pdfs end to end, so nobody has tested it with real listeners at scale.
needs_humans: at least 15 blind and low-vision people who use a screen reader every day, covering nvda, jaws and voiceover.

title: fix the 100 oldest bugs in inkscape
what: inkscape is the free drawing program that designers, teachers and hobbyists use when they can't or won't pay for illustrator, and bugs that sit open for years keep tripping them up. its development tracker has 2,119 open issues, and the oldest confirmed bugs have waited there since 2018. pick one off a frozen list, reproduce it on master and get a fix merged. the dream is 500, and this is the first hundred.
done_when: each of the 100 oldest open bugs in inkscape's development tracker (list frozen when the shwarm is posted, feature requests and design questions left out) is closed by an inkscape developer, with a merged fix or a note that it no longer happens on master.

runs.command: for i in $(cat oldest100.txt); do curl -s "https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/inkscape%2Finkscape/issues/$i" | jq -r .state; done | sort | uniq -c   # pass: '100 closed'

people.instructions: pick 10 closed bugs at random, follow the original repro steps on an inkscape master build, and confirm each one is really gone. post your build hash and a screenshot per bug.

why_now: inkscape 1.4.4 just shipped and the team is writing its ai policy right now, so careful, open help can show what good looks like.
needs_humans: daily inkscape users who can confirm a bug is really fixed, and one person the inkscape devs already know to be the crew's contact.

title: gtk2 holdouts, ported before debian drops them
what: if you rely on an older linux app like gkrellm or gerbv, it may soon vanish from debian. debian plans to remove gtk2 before debian 14, and 77 packages, gkrellm and gerbv among them, still have open bugs saying they depend on it. we port them to gtk3 or gtk4, or they leave the archive.
done_when: at least 30 of the open 'depends on deprecated gtk 2' bugs in debian's gtk2 usertag list are closed because the package now builds against gtk3 or gtk4.

runs.command: curl -s 'https://udd.debian.org/cgi-bin/bts-usertags.cgi?user=pkg-gnome-maintainers%40lists.alioth.debian.org&tag=gtk2' | sed 's/<[^>]*>/\n/g' | grep -cx '\s*open\s*'   # 78 on oct 7 2026; pass: 48 or lower

people.instructions: install 5 ported apps from unstable and use each for 10 minutes the way its users would. report every feature that broke compared to the gtk2 version.

why_now: debian 14 is expected in 2027, and gtk2 has had no upstream release since 2020.
needs_humans: people who use these apps and can tell when a port behaves wrong.

title: old gimp plug-ins, brought to gimp 3
what: people who leaned on gimp's old plug-ins for years find many of them missing in gimp 3. debian's gimp-plugin-registry bundles favorites like film grain and the orton glow, and the old gimp 2 plug-in registry is archived. gimp 3 changed its plug-in api, and 18 of debian's are switched off in the package. the maintainer ported seven others in early october. we pick the 100 people miss most and bring them across, each tested by someone who used it.
done_when: 100 plug-ins and scripts from the archived gimp 2 plug-in registry and debian's gimp-plugin-registry, picked by a public vote of at least 30 gimp users, each either runs in gimp 3 from a public port and is confirmed by someone who used it in gimp 2 to work as before, or is marked built into gimp 3 with the replacement named.

runs.command: python check_ports.py ports.json (for each of the 100: confirms the port loads in gimp 3's console mode, its source is public, and a tester's before-and-after comparison is linked)

people.instructions: run 10 random ported plug-ins in gimp 3 on the crew's sample photos and compare with gimp 2.10 output side by side. flag any that look different or crash.

why_now: new uploads with gimp 3 ports landed on oct 6 2026, and gimp now has an official porting guide.
needs_humans: photographers and longtime gimp users who used these plug-ins in gimp 2, to vote on the 100 and test each port, plus people who can port python and script-fu plug-ins.

title: sharex for linux, working for real
what: lots of windows users who switch to linux miss sharex, the free screenshot tool, and have to make do without it. its 'add linux support' issue has been open since 2022. the sharex team's cross-platform rewrite, xerahs, already builds for linux and is written with agents on purpose. we help it hold up on the desktops people use, tested by 20 people on their own machines and monitors.
done_when: a tagged xerahs release where 20 people across at least 8 linux desktop and distro combinations, including gnome wayland, kde wayland, hyprland and x11, with at least 3 multi-monitor and 3 hidpi setups among them, each finish the crew's 10-step capture checklist with no crash and no missing step.

people.instructions: install the tagged release on your desktop, run the published 10-step checklist (region shot, screen recording, gif, annotation, upload and the rest), and link a screen recording with your distro, desktop version and monitor setup.

why_now: linux bug reports for xerahs, like wayland recording stalls, are arriving this month, so the gaps are easy to find.
needs_humans: 20 people who run linux daily across at least 8 desktop and distro setups, some with multi-monitor and hidpi screens.
